counter_system.title: POS 1 — The Counter System: Concepts & Architecture
counter_system.desc: The foundation of the ZhiftPOS certification: the four parts of the system and the local-copy design, the Point of Sale Profile as the counter's rulebook, the five user roles with per-permission Power Approvers, the selling modes, what a completed sale creates, and the counter problems each feature is designed to prevent — opening the Okelewo Stores case study.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — What this track certifies
lessons.html:
This track certifies you on ZhiftPOS: the point of sale system used at the counter. By the end of the eight modules you will be able to configure a counter correctly, run a trading day on it, handle discounts, returns, vouchers and the special counters, keep selling when the network is down, and check the counter's figures at the end of every day.

The design principle. ZhiftPOS is built on one design principle: the counter is governed centrally and trades locally. Governed centrally means that everything a cashier is allowed to do — discounting, refunding cash, selling on credit, which payment methods appear — is decided in the back office on a record called the Point of Sale Profile, not at the till and not by habit. Trades locally means the till keeps its own copy of the product catalogue, prices and stock on the terminal, so scanning is instant and selling continues even when the internet connection drops completely.

Why the counter needs this much care. The counter is where the business handles the most money with the least supervision. Every naira of retail revenue passes through a cashier's hands before it appears anywhere else. It is also where most retail losses happen: unrecorded discounts, refunds without goods coming back, cash missing from a drawer nobody counted. ZhiftPOS is designed so that each of these has a control built into the software. This track teaches you the controls, how to set them up, and how to read the reports that show whether they are working.

The eight modules. Module 1 (this one) covers the parts of the system, the user roles, and the selling modes. Module 2 covers the Point of Sale Profile in full — it is the most important record in the system, so it gets ten chapters. Module 3 covers installing and licensing terminals and setting up hardware. Module 4 covers the trading day: opening a shift, building sales, taking payment, closing the shift. Module 5 covers discounts, returns and overrides. Module 6 covers Lay-By, Staff Purchase, Airtime and the Customer Desk. Module 7 covers the gift voucher programme. Module 8 covers offline behaviour, the sales queue, end-of-day checking and supervision — it also gets ten chapters, because checking the counter's work matters as much as setting it up.

The case study. Throughout the track you will follow Okelewo Stores, a retailer with three branches — a flagship on Okelewo Lalubu Road in Abeokuta, a second Abeokuta shop, and one in Lagos. At the start of the track Okelewo runs its counters on exercise books and one old till. By the end, all three branches run on ZhiftPOS. Each module shows one stage of that journey, so you can see every feature being used in a real shop, with real problems.

Each module ends with a module rule. A module rule is a one-sentence statement that sums the module up. Module rule 1: the counter runs on a profile, not on memory. You will meet the other seven as you go.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The four parts of ZhiftPOS
lessons.html:
ZhiftPOS has four parts, and knowing what each one does explains most of how the till behaves.

1. The back office. The central web system where items, prices, stock, customers, invoices and accounts live. Administrators configure POS Profiles, promotions, vouchers and staff access here, and finance sees every posted sale here. Prices and policy flow down from the back office to the tills; completed sales flow up from the tills to the back office.

2. The till application. The desktop application installed on each counter terminal. This is what cashiers use: the Sales Console and the other counter screens such as Return & Exchange, Lay-By and Sales History. It is an installed Windows application, not a web page — this matters, because an installed application can keep working with its own local data when the network cannot reach the server.

3. The background sync service. A service installed alongside the till application. It starts when the terminal starts and keeps running even when nobody is signed in. It has two jobs: it keeps the terminal's local copy of the catalogue, prices and stock up to date, and it holds the queue of completed sales that are waiting to post to the back office.

4. The terminal management service. An optional head-office component for monitoring and managing all the terminals in the business: seeing which tills are online, pushing settings, retiring a terminal that has been lost or replaced. Module 3 covers it.

Why ZhiftPOS keeps a local copy. The till is not a browser window onto the server. It keeps its own copy of products, prices and stock on the terminal. This is why scanning is instant even on a slow connection, and why selling continues when the connection drops completely: completed sales queue on the terminal and post automatically when the link returns.

Three practical consequences of this design, worth memorising now:

• Queued sales are safe. A sale that has been completed but not yet posted sits in the queue on the terminal. Closing the application or restarting the terminal does not lose it. When the connection returns, the queue posts on its own.

• Never shut a terminal down to force a sync. Because the sync service runs whether or not anyone is signed in, a terminal left switched on overnight still receives price changes and still posts its queued sales. Restarting achieves nothing that waiting does not, and while the terminal is off, nothing syncs at all.

• Local copies age. The prices and stock figures on the till are the local copy's figures. The top bar shows Stock stale or Price stale indicators when the copies need refreshing, and a Sync button to refresh them on demand. Module 8 covers reading these indicators in detail.

How the parts fit together in one sentence. The back office decides policy and holds the books; the till trades using its local copy; the sync service moves data between them in both directions; and the terminal management service watches the whole fleet.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Point of Sale Profile: a first look
lessons.html:
The most important record in ZhiftPOS is the Point of Sale Profile. One profile governs one counter's entire behaviour. Module 2 walks through every field on it; this chapter explains what kind of record it is and why so much depends on it.

What the profile decides. Almost every question about what a cashier can or cannot do at a counter is answered by a field on that counter's profile. Examples:

• Whether a cashier can give a discount at all, and under which of three discount modes.
• Whether a refund can be paid in cash, or only as store credit.
• Whether a shift must be opened before anything can be sold.
• Which payment methods appear on the payment screen, and in what order.
• Whether the counter sells gift vouchers, takes lay-bys, allows staff purchases, or checks customer credit limits.
• Who is allowed to approve the things a cashier cannot do alone.

Policy enforced by the system, not by supervision. In a shop without ZhiftPOS, rules like these live in people's heads: the discount rule is verbal, the returns rule depends on which supervisor is present, and the rules hold only while someone senior is watching. On ZhiftPOS the rules are settings. A discount control that is disabled on the profile is disabled for everyone, at every hour, whether or not a supervisor is on the floor. This is the practical meaning of governed centrally: the policy is enforced by the software itself.

The disabled control explains itself. When a control is disabled, hovering over it shows a tooltip stating why — for example that discounts are disabled on this profile, or that no approvers are configured. This means a cashier can read the reason directly from the screen instead of guessing, and can give the customer an accurate answer.

The first troubleshooting rule. Learn this rule now, because it answers a large share of everyday support questions: if a menu item is missing from a cashier's sidebar, check the profile before anything else. A missing console almost always means one of two things — the feature is switched off on the profile, or the cashier's row in the profile's user table does not grant them access to it. It is almost never a fault. Check the relevant profile tab first, then the cashier's user row. Module 2 shows exactly where each setting lives.

One profile per counter, or one per shop? A profile can serve one till or be shared by several. The rule of thumb: use one shared profile when every till in a shop should behave identically — there is less to maintain, and each terminal is still identified individually in reports. Use separate profiles when tills genuinely need different rules — for example a dedicated returns desk with different permissions. In short: the number of profiles should match the number of different policies, not the number of terminals.

What to remember from this chapter. The profile is the counter's rulebook, the system enforces it automatically, disabled controls state their reason, and the profile is always your first stop when something seems to be missing.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The five user roles
lessons.html:
ZhiftPOS access is controlled by five roles. Roles are assigned to user accounts in the back office, and one person can hold more than one role — common in smaller businesses.

1. Point of Sale Administrator. Sets up and maintains the system: creates and edits POS Profiles, adds cashiers, sets discount policy, configures printers and other hardware, commissions new terminals, and installs updates. The administrator can reach everything, including the System Settings screen on the till itself.

2. Sales Manager. Supervises trading: watches sales through the day, approves overrides, runs end-of-day reports, and reconciles shifts. The Sales Manager can reach the Command Center and Revenue Intelligence screens in addition to the selling screens. Module 8 covers this role's daily and weekly work in detail.

3. Cashier. Serves customers: opens a shift, sells, takes payment, handles returns if permitted, and closes the shift. A cashier reaches the selling consoles their profile grants them, plus Sales History, Customer Desk and Inventory Ops. Module 4 is written for this role.

4. Power Approver. Authorises the sensitive actions a cashier cannot perform alone. Each approver is granted specific permissions from a set of five: Discount, Returns, Clear Cart, Rate, and Credit Limit Override. The permissions are separate tick-boxes — a person who can approve returns cannot approve a price change unless that box is also ticked. An approver authorises at the till in one of two ways: by entering their email and password, or by a six-digit one-time code that the system emails to every approver who holds the relevant permission. Codes expire after one hour. Every approval is recorded: who approved, what, and when.

5. Voucher Manager. Runs the gift voucher programme: creates voucher batches, sets voucher branding, and monitors the outstanding voucher liability. This role exists because vouchers are money — from the moment one is sold, the business owes its value to whoever holds it — so creating them needs a specifically responsible person. Module 7 covers the role's work.

One person, one account. The single most important access rule in this track: every cashier must have their own account, and accounts are never shared. Every record ZhiftPOS keeps — sales, overrides, shift closes, variances — is attributed to the signed-in account. If four cashiers share one login, every record says the same name, and none of the controls in this track can tell you who actually did anything. When several cashiers share a physical terminal, they still use individual accounts: the lock button in the top bar lets one cashier lock the till and the next unlock it with their own credentials in seconds. In the Okelewo case study, giving every cashier their own account is the first thing done — before any other setup.

Where roles are checked. If a person cannot see or do something you expect them to, check in this order: their role on the user account, then their row in the profile's user table, then the profile setting for the feature itself. This is the Chapter 3 rule extended one step.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The selling modes
lessons.html:
Every POS Profile is set to one selling mode. The mode decides which consoles appear on the till and how a sale flows from basket to payment. There are three modes in the retail edition, plus one separate edition.

Standard. One person builds the basket and takes the payment, on the Sales Console. This is the ordinary shop counter, and the mode most of this track assumes.

Pharmacy. A two-stage flow for counters where the person who assembles the order and the person who collects payment are different people. Stage one: an Order Console, where an order is built and handed off. Stage two: a Checkout Console, where a second person collects the payment. This mode is standard practice in pharmacies, where a dispenser prepares the medicines and a cashier handles the money, but it is useful anywhere you want the goods and the money handled by different hands: the person who picked the items never touches the payment, and the person who takes the payment did not pick the items. Note one access detail: the Checkout role also carries access to Revenue Intelligence, the money reports.

Booking. A reserve-first flow. A sales representative reserves goods for a customer against a draft bill on the Booking Console; a cashier later collects payment and releases the goods on the Cashier Console. This suits showrooms and negotiated sales, where the customer agrees today and pays later. It replaces the informal habit of keeping something aside for a customer from memory: the reservation is a record, and the payment completes it.

Restaurant. Table service with a kitchen display is handled by a separate restaurant edition of ZhiftPOS. The retail edition covered by this track does not include it.

Three rules about modes.

Rule 1 — set the mode first. When you create a profile, choose the mode before doing anything else. The mode controls which access boxes in the profile's user table are meaningful, and the system normalises those boxes against the mode when the profile is saved. If you fill in the user table first and change the mode afterwards, the access boxes are reset to match the new mode and your earlier work is undone.

Rule 2 — change a live profile's mode only outside trading hours. For the same reason: switching the mode resets the user table's access boxes. Do it after close, then re-check every cashier's row before the next day's trading.

Rule 3 — the licence's mode wins. Each branch's licence also carries a selling mode, and the licence's mode takes precedence over the profile's. A shop licensed for Standard shows the Standard console even if its profile says Pharmacy. Two practical consequences: when planning a two-stage counter, confirm the licence supports it before building the profile; and when a counter shows different consoles from what the profile says, check the licence — that is usually the answer. Module 3 covers licensing fully.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — What happens when a sale completes
lessons.html:
To troubleshoot a till and to check its figures, you need to know what a completed sale actually creates. This chapter follows one sale through the system.

1. An invoice is created. Every completed sale becomes a sales invoice with a reference number, its item lines, and its payments. There is no such thing as an off-record sale on ZhiftPOS: if it went through the till, there is an invoice.

2. A receipt is printed. The receipt carries the sale's reference and a barcode. Receipts can be reprinted later from the Recent Receipts panel or from Sales History, so a customer who loses a receipt is not a dead end.

3. The sale posts, or queues. If the terminal is online, the sale posts to the back office within moments. If the terminal is offline, the sale joins the queue and posts when the connection returns. An offline sale prints its receipt with a local reference; once the sale posts, it also has a back-office invoice number. Both references point to the same sale, and a return can be found using either one. An offline receipt is a fully valid receipt.

4. Stock is reduced. The sold quantities come off the profile's warehouse. If the item is batch-tracked or serial-numbered, the specific batch or serial recorded on the sale is the one deducted — this is what makes returns, warranty claims and recalls traceable to the exact unit.

5. Cash lands in the drawer, inside a shift. Where shift management is enabled, every sale happens inside a shift that was opened with a counted float and will be closed with a counted drawer. The shift is what connects the physical cash to the recorded sales. Module 4 covers the full ritual.

The drawer is the cashier's responsibility. ZhiftPOS treats the drawer as something a cashier takes over and hands back: you count what you receive at the start (the opening float), everything you take in or pay out during the shift is recorded against your sales, and you count what you hand back at the close. The difference between what the system expects and what you count is the variance, and it is attributed to your shift. This is protective in both directions: it makes a shortage traceable, and it clears the cashier whose counts match.

Returns are linked to the original sale. A return on ZhiftPOS always starts by finding the original invoice — by scanning the receipt barcode or entering either reference. There is no way to process a return against nothing. The reason is simple: a refund with no original sale behind it is indistinguishable from money simply leaving the drawer, so the system requires the link. Module 5 covers the full returns flow.

Connections to the rest of ZhiftERP. Because the till posts real invoices into the same system the business runs on, the counter's data flows onward without re-typing: staff purchases feed payroll deduction, the day's takings feed the bank reconciliation, stock movements feed inventory, and every figure a manager reads in Revenue Intelligence is built from the same invoices. Nothing at the counter is a side record.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The problems ZhiftPOS is designed to prevent
lessons.html:
Each major feature of ZhiftPOS exists because of a specific, common problem at retail counters. Knowing the problems makes the features make sense — and helps you explain, during rollout, why the system works the way it does.

The exercise book. Sales written in a notebook, prices from memory, the day's total whatever the book says. There is no line-level record (which item, which price), stock is never reduced, and any dispute comes down to a pencil line against a customer's word. ZhiftPOS answers this with the invoice: every sale recorded line by line, stock reduced automatically, every receipt reprintable.

The shared login. One account used by four cashiers. Every sale, override and variance says the same name, so nothing can be attributed to anyone. This one problem disables almost every control in the system, which is why one-person-one-account (Chapter 4) always comes first. The lock button makes individual accounts practical even on a shared terminal.

The memory price and the mood discount. Prices that live in the seller's head and drift from day to day; discounts given by feel, recorded nowhere, added up by no one. ZhiftPOS answers with the price list (every item's price is a record with a validity period) and the discount modes (every discount needs a mode, and depending on the mode, a reason and an approver). Module 5 covers this fully.

The unreconciled drawer. A float nobody counted, a close nobody checked, a drawer that is about right. A counter that never reconciles cannot tell error from theft, so it quietly suffers both. ZhiftPOS answers with shift management: counted float at open, counted drawer at close, variance calculated per payment method and explained in notes.

The phantom return and the quiet void. Two classic counter frauds. A phantom return: a refund is processed with no customer and no goods — cash leaves the drawer against a fictional return. A quiet void: a customer pays, then the sale is voided or the cart cleared after they leave, and the cash is pocketed. ZhiftPOS puts a wall in front of each: returns must start from a found invoice, carry a reason, and can require an approver; clearing a cart can itself require approval; and voids and cleared carts are recorded and reportable per cashier. Module 8's fraud chapter shows what to check.

The disconnected till. A shop that has a till, but the till stands alone: its sales are retyped into the books weekly, its stock never updates live. The double entry breeds errors and delay. ZhiftPOS answers with the architecture of Chapter 2: the till posts real invoices into the central system as sales complete.

A useful question. When assessing any counter — including before a ZhiftPOS rollout — ask: when a sale completes here, what else happens, and when? On a well-run ZhiftPOS counter the answer is Chapter 6: an invoice, a receipt, a stock movement, a posting, all immediately. Any other answer points to one of the problems above.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: Okelewo Stores before ZhiftPOS
lessons.html:
Okelewo Stores is the retailer this track follows. This chapter records where they start, so the later modules mean something concrete.

The business. Three branches: the flagship on Okelewo Lalubu Road in Abeokuta, a second, smaller Abeokuta shop, and one shop in Lagos. Eleven counter staff across the three. The founder and MD has run the business for nine years, largely by personal presence and long hours.

The counters, before. The two smaller branches run on exercise books. The flagship has an old standalone till — and all four of its cashiers share one login. Prices differ between branches because they live in people's memories; in one recorded week the same item sold at three different prices across the three shops. The drawers are counted irregularly; day totals disagree with the cash by amounts nobody can break down, and about right has become the accepted standard four days out of five.

Two incidents from the last month before rollout. First: a refund was given twice with no receipt presented and nothing written down — one was probably genuine; nobody can say about the other, and that is exactly the problem. Second: the flagship's till showed a pattern of returns the MD found suspicious, but because the login is shared, the records could not point to a person — so the suspicion landed on everyone and settled on no one. The MD's summary at the first project meeting: I built three shops and I cannot tell you what any counter did on Tuesday. I am done managing by suspicion.

The rollout decision. Okelewo adopts ZhiftPOS across all three branches. The roles are assigned as follows, using Chapter 4's role set:

• The operations lead becomes the Point of Sale Administrator — she already administers the company's ZhiftERP system, so the counter's configuration joins her existing responsibilities.
• The flagship's senior supervisor becomes the Sales Manager. Module 8 will test this role hardest.
• Four staff across the branches become Power Approvers, each with only the permission boxes they need. Deliberately, the Returns permission is not given to everyone who holds the Discount permission — approving a discount and approving money leaving the drawer are different responsibilities.
• The accountant becomes the Voucher Manager, ahead of the voucher programme launching in module 7. Vouchers are money the business will owe, so they are put with the person who manages money.
• Every one of the eleven cashiers gets their own account, with a working email address, before anything else is configured. The shared login is retired on day one.

The plan, module by module. Module 2: build the three profiles (one per branch, since each branch's tills will follow one policy). Module 3: replace the flagship's old till, commission terminals at all branches, sort licences and hardware. Module 4: introduce shift management with counted floats. Module 5: set up discount rules, approvers in practice, and the returns desk. Module 6: launch Lay-By (customers have been asking), Staff Purchase, and Airtime. Module 7: launch the gift voucher programme for December. Module 8: put the end-of-day checks and weekly reviews in place, and hand the MD a short page of numbers to replace the suspicion. The MD's closing line from the kickoff: so the counter gets rules, a routine, and a daily check. Nine years late. Begin.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & module rule 1
lessons.html:
This module set the foundations. Before the quiz, check yourself against each of these. If any feels unclear, re-read its chapter — the rest of the track builds on all of them.

The four parts (Chapter 2). Back office (policy and books), till application (the cashier's screens), background sync service (local copies and the sales queue, running whether or not anyone is signed in), terminal management service (fleet monitoring). And the design idea underneath: the till keeps a local copy, so selling is fast and survives network failure, and completed sales queue safely until they post. Never restart a terminal to force a sync — the service catches up on its own.

The profile (Chapter 3). One profile governs one counter. Every counter power is a profile setting, enforced by the software at all hours. Disabled controls show their reason on hover. First troubleshooting rule: a missing menu item means check the profile and the user's row on it, not a fault. Number of profiles = number of different policies.

The roles (Chapter 4). POS Administrator (configures), Sales Manager (supervises and reconciles), Cashier (serves), Power Approver (authorises specific actions — five separate permission boxes, approval by password or one-hour emailed code), Voucher Manager (runs the voucher programme). And the rule that everything else depends on: one person, one account, always — shared logins make every record anonymous and every control useless. Use the lock button between cashiers on a shared terminal.

The modes (Chapter 5). Standard (one person sells and collects), Pharmacy (Order Console then Checkout Console — goods and money in different hands), Booking (reserve first, pay later), Restaurant (separate edition). Set the mode first; change it only out of hours and re-check the user table; and remember the licence's mode overrides the profile's.

The sale (Chapter 6). A completed sale creates an invoice, prints a reprintable receipt, posts or queues, reduces stock (down to the batch or serial), and lands its cash inside a counted shift. Offline sales carry a local reference and later a back-office number — both find the same sale. Returns always start from the original invoice.

The problems (Chapter 7). Exercise book, shared login, memory prices, unreconciled drawer, phantom return and quiet void, disconnected till — and the feature that answers each. Plus the assessment question: when a sale completes here, what else happens, and when?

The case (Chapter 8). Okelewo Stores: three branches, exercise books and a shared-login till, a suspicious returns pattern that could not be attributed, and a rollout plan that starts by giving every cashier their own account.

Module rule 1: the counter runs on a profile, not on memory. Policy lives in settings the system enforces, every action is attributed to an individual account, and every sale is a record. Module 2 opens the profile itself — every tab, every field.
