shift_sale.title: POS 4 — Shift Operations & Sales Processing
shift_sale.desc: The trading day: sign-in and the top-bar indicators, opening the shift with a counted float, building sales with stack/queue and the line markers, batches/serials/units done accurately, customers, loyalty and the credit suspension, hold versus clear and every payment method's rules, receipts, the gift voucher sale and the till lock, and closing the shift against pre-filled figures that are counted, overwritten and explained.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Signing in and reading the screen
lessons.html:
This module covers the trading day from sign-in to shift close. It is the cashier's module: if any part of this track is printed and kept at the counter, it is this one. The module rule: the shift is a sealed routine — count at open, count at close, explain every variance.

Signing in. Three ways, depending on circumstances:

• Normal. Email and password. The till loads your profile, catalogue and permissions, and opens on the first console your access row grants. A forgotten password is reset by email — the terminal must be online for the reset.
• Offline. Where the profile enables it, you can sign in against the terminal's stored record when the server is unreachable — provided you have signed in online on this terminal within the last seven days. The top bar shows an Offline login marker. Practical rule: sign in online at least weekly on every terminal you use, or an outage will lock you out at the worst time.
• Manager override. If offline sign-in is refused because the terminal has no record of you, a manager can sign you in on their credentials. The sales in that session are tagged for audit, and you are told so at the time.

The top bar. Learn to read these indicators — each one is either fine, something you click, or something you report:

• Online / Offline — whether the terminal can reach the back office.
• Offline login — you signed in locally; reports and server lookups wait for the connection.
• Queued — completed sales waiting to post. They are safe; they post automatically when online.
• Re-login — a cashier's stored credentials were rejected. If it names you: click it and sign in online, or your queued sales cannot post.
• Conflicts — sales held back because a batch or serial is no longer available. Click to resolve (module 8).
• Stock stale / Price stale — the local copies need refreshing. Click to sync.
• Failed — sales the back office rejected; a supervisor handles these (module 8).
• Duty — Active or Inactive, with the shift button beside it (shown where shift management is on).
• Also: store, date, time, your name and role; the envelope (Message Hub, with unread count); Sync (refresh now — hover shows when each copy last updated); the padlock (lock the till); Sign out.

The Sales Console. Products on the left with the search box above; the current order on the right. The cart header shows the customer and the item/quantity counts — and, where credit checking is on, the customer's balance and limit. The footer shows sales total, discount, subtotal, tax, delivery fee if enabled, and net total, with the payment buttons beneath. The sidebar lists the consoles your row grants. Below it: card/list view (list fits more), product images on or off (off is noticeably faster), items per row, and Recent receipts for quick reprints.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Opening the shift
lessons.html:
Where shift management is enabled, you must open a shift before you can sell. Opening takes two minutes; doing it properly is what makes the end of the day painless.

Procedure.

1. Click the clock icon in the top bar. The Open Shift window appears.
2. Count the float — physically count the money in the drawer.
3. Enter the counted amount against each payment method. Cash is normally the only one with an opening amount; leave the others at zero.
4. Add an opening note if anything is unusual — a short float, a missing key.
5. Click Open Shift. The Duty indicator turns Active.

Why the count matters. The opening amount is what your closing count will be measured against. If you type a round number instead of counting — entering 20,000 because that is what the float should be, when the drawer actually holds 19,400 — then even a perfect day ends 600 short, and the evening is spent investigating a shortage that never happened. Worse, if that becomes normal, real shortages hide inside the always-a-bit-off habit. Thirty seconds of counting buys an evening of certainty. Note: a short float declared in the opening note is context; the same shortfall discovered at close is a dispute.

Float preparation. The float should be prepared before the shift — counted denominations suitable for change-making, sealed until the drawer is loaded. Preparing floats is a supervisor task on module 8's calendar; counting what you receive is yours.

Handover during the day. When one cashier hands a till to another mid-day, run it as two shifts: the first cashier closes their shift with a full count; the second opens a new shift with their own count. Never pass one open shift between people — a shared shift produces a shared variance, and a shared variance cannot be attributed to anyone. One person, one shift, one drawer, one count.

If a shift was never opened. Sales rung with no shift open are not attached to any shift, which is why they later seem to be missing from shift summaries. The repair is the back-office orphaned transactions tool, which attaches them to the shift they belong to — a supervisor task, and a correction, not a normal workflow. If you find yourself selling and Duty shows Inactive, stop and open a shift first.

Summary. Count before you open. Declare anything unusual in the note. Handover means two shifts. Never sell without a shift open.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Building a sale
lessons.html:
Items go into the cart three ways, and the cart has a small set of rules worth knowing precisely.

Adding items.

• Scan the barcode. The item goes straight into the cart — the search box does not need to be selected first, so scanning works even mid-conversation.
• Search by name, code or brand, then pick from the results.
• Tap a tile in the product grid.

Stack or queue. Where the profile enables the item queue option, a toggle beside the search box selects the behaviour: stack — re-scanning an item increases its existing line; queue — every scan makes its own line, used where each unit needs its own serial or batch entry.

Editing quantities. Each line has minus and plus buttons and an editable quantity box. Type the number and press Enter to apply it; press Escape to abandon the edit. Use the keys — a half-typed quantity left unconfirmed is how a wrong quantity rides through to payment.

Removing lines. The bin icon removes a line. Exceptions with fixed behaviour:

• Bonus items (from promotions), bundle components, and gift voucher lines have fixed quantities and cannot be edited line by line.
• Bundle components cannot be removed individually — remove the bundle's main line, and the components go with it. The bundle price governs its parts (module 5 covers bundles).

Line markers. Small labels on cart lines record what has happened to them:

• Bundle — the line heads a bundle.
• Rate override — the price was manually changed. Visible on review, deliberately.
• Customer discount — a discount recorded on the customer's record applied automatically.
• Batch assigned — batches have been selected for the line (clickable — see Chapter 4).

Read the markers before taking payment: a line carrying a promotion will refuse a manual discount, and the marker tells you why before the error message does. Supervisors read the same markers when reviewing sales.

Before payment: the ten-second check. Glance at the footer — item count, quantity count, net total — against what is on the counter and what the customer expects. On multi-unit items, check the unit (Chapter 4). Read any markers you did not put there yourself. A wrong quantity caught in the cart costs a keystroke; caught at payment it costs a correction; caught after the customer leaves it costs a return, an approval and an explanation.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Batches, serials and units of measure
lessons.html:
Items tracked by batch or serial, and items sold in more than one unit, add a step to the sale. The step is quick — and it is the whole point of the tracking.

Batch-tracked items. When you add a batch-tracked item, the till asks which batch the goods come from, showing available batches and quantities.

• A quantity can be split across batches — allocate part against one batch, part against another.
• Where the profile enables auto-allocate, the till picks batches for you, oldest first, and only asks when the quantity cannot be covered from one batch.
• Reducing a line's quantity releases batch allocations in reverse order — the last-allocated batch is released first.
• The Batch assigned marker on the line is clickable: use it to review or change the selection before payment.

Practical rule: make sure the batches on the sale match the goods actually going into the bag. With auto-allocate on, the till picks the oldest batch — if you physically picked from the front of the shelf, click the marker and correct it. Expiry tracking only works when the record and the bag agree.

Serial-numbered items. Serial-tracked items require one serial per unit, scanned or typed into the serial window. The line cannot proceed to payment until every unit has a serial.

Practical rule: scan the serials from the units in the bag — the actual items being handed over — never from a convenient box on the shelf. The serial ties this physical unit to this sale; warranty claims, returns and recalls all depend on that link being true. A serial record that does not match the goods handed over is worse than no record.

Units of measure. Where an item sells in more than one unit (each, pack, carton), the till asks which unit applies, and the price follows the unit chosen.

Practical rule: check the unit on multi-unit lines during the ten-second footer check. A carton sold at the single-unit price is a large, silent discount nobody approved — it looks normal on screen and only surfaces later in the margin figures.

When a batch or serial is refused. Occasionally the till refuses a batch or serial because another terminal sold it in the meantime. This is normal on a multi-till or offline estate: pick a different batch or serial and continue. If a completed sale is held back for this reason, it appears under the Conflicts indicator in the top bar; resolving conflicts is covered in module 8 — the short version is that a conflict is fixed by re-picking, and conflicts are cleared before the shift closes.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Customers, loyalty and credit at the counter
lessons.html:
A sale with no customer attached books to the walk-in customer, which is correct for most of the queue. Attach a named customer when the sale involves loyalty, credit, a delivery, or a customer who asks to be on record.

Attaching a customer. Use the person icon above the grid or the customer chip on the cart header, then:

• Search by name, phone or email and select. Offline, the search runs against the terminal's cached customer list.
• Create a new customer — name, plus mobile and email if available. Two protections from module 2 apply here: duplicate names may be refused (if the profile says so), and a new customer whose mobile number matches an existing record merges into it automatically.
• Scan a loyalty card using the scan button above the grid — the member loads automatically and their points appear on the header.

What attaching does immediately:

• Any discount recorded on the customer's record applies to the cart (the Customer discount marker) — recorded policy, applied automatically.
• Where credit checking is on, the customer's balance and credit limit appear on the cart header.

Habit: attach the customer before scanning items whenever the sale is clearly a member's or an account customer's. Attaching late still applies discounts correctly to what is in the cart, but attaching after payment is too late for points — which becomes a dispute and a reprint request together.

The credit suspension. A customer over their credit limit shows Sales suspended due to customer outstanding on the cart, and payment is blocked. Only a Power Approver holding the Credit Limit Override permission can release it — a recorded approval.

How to handle the moment: state it as the system's rule, not your judgment — the account needs a supervisor's approval before more can be added to it. If the customer prefers, a fully paid cash sale needs no release at all. Do not work around the suspension by splitting the purchase across tickets or under-recording it — module 8 treats exactly that pattern as a red flag, and the approval takes a minute.

Loyalty at the counter. Three facts:

• Earning requires attachment. A member not attached to the sale earns nothing — attaching is the programme.
• Redemption happens at payment and needs the terminal online, because the points balance lives on the server.
• Returns interact with points. If the original sale earned points that have since been spent, the return calculates what must be recovered and shows it before completion — read the figure from the screen to the customer; never estimate it (module 5 covers returns).

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Hold, clear, and taking payment
lessons.html:
Hold versus Clear. Two different actions with different consequences:

• Hold parks the basket and clears the screen for the next customer. A held basket keeps its customer, discounts and batch allocations. Resume it from the box icon above the grid, which shows the count of held baskets. Old held baskets age out automatically where the profile's housekeeping is set.
• Clear discards the basket entirely. Where the profile does not permit the cashier to clear but an approver holds the Clear Cart permission, the Clear button appears but requires an approval.

Rule: hold, do not clear. The customer who steps away to fetch a wallet gets a hold — clearing throws away the batch and serial work already done. And because building a basket, taking cash, then clearing it is a known fraud pattern, cleared carts are recorded and reviewed (module 8); the honest habit is simply to hold.

Cash. Press Cash, enter the amount tendered (or tap a quick-amount button). The till calculates and displays the change, completes the sale, opens the drawer, and prints per configuration.

Card. Without an integrated terminal, the till simply records the card amount — process the card on the machine as usual, then confirm. With an integrated terminal (module 2, Tab 5), the amount is pushed to the device and the till waits for the result.

Split payment. One bill across several methods:

1. Turn on Split payment in the payment window.
2. Choose a method and enter its portion.
3. Add another method for each further portion, watching the remaining balance fall.
4. Complete when the remaining balance reaches zero.

Over-tender rule: if cash is among the methods, over-tendering shows change due; without cash, the total cannot exceed the amount owed.

Record every portion on its true method. Recording a transfer as cash to finish faster creates two wrong figures at the close — cash over and transfer short — from one sale.

Server-verified tenders. Three tenders need the terminal online, because the balance they draw on lives on the server:

• Loyalty redemption — Redeem Loyalty Points, choose the programme, enter the points; their cash value is deducted.
• Gift vouchers — added in the payment window's voucher section, scanned or typed. More than one voucher can be applied; if vouchers cover the whole bill no other tender is needed; any surplus follows the profile's change policy.
• Store credit — chosen as a payment method; the available balance is shown, and an amount above it is refused.

Offline payment summary. Cash, manually keyed card, and transfer work offline. Integrated card, store credit, loyalty redemption, vouchers (unless Guarded Offline is configured), and any credit or part-paid sale do not — offline, collect the full amount.

Back-dating. Where the profile allows transaction date editing, a date field appears at the top of the payment window — today or earlier only. Use it only for a genuinely late-entered sale; it moves revenue between reporting days, which is why the permission is granted sparingly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Receipts, selling a gift voucher, and locking the till
lessons.html:
Receipts. Where auto-print is on, the receipt prints on completion (one or two copies per the printer settings); otherwise print from the confirmation screen. Reprints: the Recent receipts panel (from the catalogue controls) covers the last few sales; Sales History (module 6) covers anything older.

Offline references. A sale completed offline prints its receipt with a local reference. When the sale posts, it also receives a back-office invoice number. Both numbers refer to the same sale, and a return can be found using either one. An offline receipt is a fully valid document — say so with confidence if a customer asks.

Selling a gift voucher. The procedure:

1. Tap the Gift Voucher tile on the product grid.
2. Choose a face value from the denomination buttons, or type another amount.
3. Set the quantity. Same-value vouchers group onto one line (a fixed-quantity line).
4. For pre-printed voucher stock, scan each physical card so its code binds to the value. For system-issued vouchers, leave codes blank — they are generated when the sale completes.
5. Attach a named customer — required, because the voucher may need emailing or reprinting later. If no email is on file the till prompts for one; it can be skipped, but then the printed slip is the only copy.
6. Take payment. Rule: vouchers are bought with cash-equivalent tenders only — never with another voucher, store credit, or loyalty points. Stored value cannot be used to create stored value.

The slip is the money. The full voucher code is printed on the slip exactly once. A reprint requires authorisation. Handle unissued and issued slips like cash, because to whoever holds one, that is what it is. Hand the slip over with that sentence — customers keep them more carefully when told.

Locking the till. The padlock in the top bar locks the terminal:

• The shift stays open.
• The basket stays exactly as it is.
• Synchronisation continues in the background.
• Unlocking takes a username and password.

Lock the till every time you step away, even for a moment. It is faster than signing out and back in, it protects the open basket (the batch and serial work, the attached customer), and it protects you: an unattended, unlocked till trades under your name — its sales, its overrides and its variances become yours regardless of whose hands made them. On shared terminals, the lock is also how cashiers change over quickly between their own accounts (module 1's one-person-one-account rule).

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Closing the shift; worked example: Okelewo's first month
lessons.html:
Closing the shift.

1. Click the clock icon. The Close Shift window shows the shift's totals — sales, returns, transaction count, and lay-by activity if there was any.
2. The counted-amount fields arrive pre-filled with what the system expects for each payment method. Do not accept these figures blindly.
3. Count the drawer and each method's takings. Overwrite each pre-filled figure with what you actually counted.
4. The variance appears beside each method — green for over, red for short — with a total at the bottom.
5. Explain any variance in the closing notes (for example: 200 over — suspected change error on a busy split sale around 4pm).
6. Click Close Shift. Duty turns Inactive.

Why not accept the pre-filled figures? The pre-fill is the system's expectation, not a count. Accepting it untouched just confirms the system against itself and proves nothing about the drawer. The counted close is what makes the shift's record real — and a variance explained in one sentence at close is far cheaper than the same variance investigated days later, when nobody remembers the busy split sale at 4pm.

Unclosed shifts. An unclosed shift leaves its sales unattributed until a supervisor reconciles them after the fact with the back-office orphaned-transactions tool. Report a missed close rather than hiding it — the tool exists as a correction, and the pattern is visible either way.

Okelewo's first month on shifts. Four events from the first month, each matching a chapter:

• Week 2 — the counted float pays off. The flagship's Tuesday drawer opens 1,500 short of the prepared float. Because the cashier counts and declares it in the opening note, the cause is found the same morning: the weekend crew had raided the float box for change. Fix: floats sealed after preparation. Under the old routine, the shortfall would have surfaced at close and been argued about for an hour.
• Week 3 — hold, not clear. A customer leaves to fetch a wallet mid-sale with three serials already scanned. The basket is held, not cleared; it resumes intact ten minutes later. Rebuilding it would have meant re-scanning the serials — or worse, guessing.
• The blind close, once. On a rushed Saturday a cashier accepts the pre-filled figures untouched. The supervisor spots it the same evening — untouched closes are recognisable by their perfect zeros — and the drawer is re-counted together: 350 over, real, unexplained because uncounted. The re-count teaches the lesson better than any memo.
• The split-payment pattern. One cashier shows small, consistent cash shortages on split-payment days. The variance report narrows it in minutes: transfers being rung as cash to balance faster — Chapter 6's exact warning. A five-minute retrain ends it. Note what the report did: it turned a suspicion into a specific, fixable habit, and cleared the cashier of anything worse.

The MD's month-end note: for nine years the drawers were about right. Now I know per shift, per person, per method — and the arguments have stopped. The counting turned out to be the cheap part.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & module rule 4
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

Sign-in and the screen (Chapter 1). Normal, offline (this terminal, within seven days), and manager override (tagged for audit, cashier told). The top bar: Online/Offline, Offline login, Queued (safe, posts automatically), Re-login (that cashier's queued sales cannot post until they sign in online), Conflicts, Stock/Price stale, Failed, Duty and the shift button, Message Hub, Sync, the padlock, Sign out. Console layout: products left, order right, totals in the footer, consoles per your access row.

Opening (Chapter 2). Count the float physically; enter it per method; declare anything unusual in the opening note. The opening figure is what the close is measured against — a typed round number manufactures variances. Handover = two shifts, two counts. Never sell with Duty Inactive; orphaned sales need the back-office repair tool.

The cart (Chapter 3). Scan (no focus needed), search, or tap. Stack vs queue. Enter applies a quantity, Escape abandons it. Bonus, bundle-component and voucher lines are fixed; remove a bundle by its main line. Markers: Bundle, Rate override, Customer discount, Batch assigned. Ten-second footer check before payment.

Tracked items (Chapter 4). Batches: split allowed; auto-allocate picks oldest first; reductions release in reverse; the Batch assigned marker reviews the pick — make the record match the bag. Serials: one per unit, from the units in the bag, and the line will not reach payment without them. Units: the price follows the unit — check it. A refused batch/serial means another till took it: re-pick; a held-back sale shows under Conflicts.

Customers (Chapter 5). Attach by search, create (mobile-match auto-merge), or loyalty scan — before the first item when you can. Attaching applies recorded discounts and shows balance/limit. Over-limit shows Sales suspended; only a Credit Limit Override approver releases it; never split tickets around it. Earning needs attachment; redemption needs the server; returns recover spent points and show the figure first.

Payment (Chapter 6). Hold keeps everything; Clear discards and may need approval — hold, do not clear. Cash calculates change and opens the drawer. Split: each portion on its true method; over-tender only with cash in the mix. Server-verified tenders: loyalty, vouchers, store credit. Offline: collect the full amount. Back-dating: today or earlier, sparingly.

Receipts, vouchers, the lock (Chapter 7). Reprints from Recent receipts or Sales History. Offline local reference and the later invoice number find the same sale. Voucher sale: denomination, scan pre-printed cards, named customer, cash-equivalent tender only, and the slip is the money — the code prints once, reprints need authorisation. Lock every time you step away: shift open, basket kept, sync running, your name protected.

Closing (Chapter 8). Pre-filled figures are expectations, not counts: count, overwrite, explain. Green over, red short. Report missed closes.

Module rule 4: the shift is a sealed routine — count at open, count at close, explain every variance. Module 5 covers discounts, returns and overrides.

concessions_returns.title: POS 5 — Concessions, Returns & Overrides
concessions_returns.desc: Discounts and returns as controlled exceptions: the five parts of every exception, the three discount modes at the till, markdown reasons with budget percentages, the discount request cycle through category leads, promotions that lock the line and bundles retired by deactivation, rate edits and credit releases under the approval mechanics, and the Return & Exchange console's three steps with loyalty recovery.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Discounts and returns: controlled exceptions
lessons.html:
This module covers everything that reduces a price or gives money back: the three discount modes in practice, markdown reasons, the discount request cycle, promotions and bundles, rate edits, credit limit releases, and the Return & Exchange console. The module rule: every discount and every return carries a reason and an approver.

Why these belong together. A discount and a return look like different subjects, but on ZhiftPOS they share the same machinery: both are exceptions to the normal arithmetic of a sale, both use the Power Approver system, both require reasons, and both leave a record. They also share the same risk: the exception path is where margin quietly disappears, and where most counter fraud is dressed up as customer service. ZhiftPOS does not try to eliminate exceptions — a shop that can never bend loses customers it should keep — it makes every exception a recorded, authorised event.

The five parts of every exception. Every discount and every return on ZhiftPOS records the same five things. Learn the list once; you will recognise it in every screen this module covers:

1. What — the line or invoice the exception applies to.
2. Who asked — the cashier.
3. Who approved — the approver, by password or one-time code, where the profile requires one.
4. Why — the reason, chosen from a list and (in approval mode) explained.
5. The record — the marker on the line, the stamp on the invoice, or the timestamped stages of a request.

When reviewing any exception later, a missing part is the finding: a discount with no reason, a return with no original invoice, an override with no approver — these are the three most common leaks, and each one is a missing part from this list.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the three discount modes as the cashier experiences them, and what cannot be discounted. Chapter 3: markdown reasons — how to build the list and what the budget percentages do. Chapter 4: the discount request cycle in Code-based mode. Chapter 5: promotions and bundles — discounts decided centrally and applied automatically. Chapter 6: rate edits and credit limit releases, and the approval mechanics in detail. Chapter 7: the Return & Exchange console, step by step. Chapter 8: Okelewo's first quarter of discount and returns data. Chapter 9: review.

One framing to keep. Margin given away is money spent. ZhiftPOS treats it that way: someone approves the spend, the reason is recorded, and the reports show where it went. That is all this module's machinery does, in different forms.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The three discount modes at the till
lessons.html:
Module 2 covered choosing the discount mode; this chapter covers using each one at the counter.

Standard mode. Press the percentage icon on a cart line, switch between percentage and amount, enter the discount, and Apply. Two built-in limits: a percentage cannot exceed 100, and an amount cannot exceed the line's rate — a discount can never turn a price negative. If the profile requires an override, the approver clears it at the moment of discounting, by password or one-time code.

Approval-based mode. The same discount window, with two required fields added:

• Discount reason — chosen from the markdown reason list.
• Explanation — typed free text.

Neither field can be left blank. The reason is stored on the sale line and appears in markdown reporting, so month-end figures show not just how much was discounted, but why. Two working habits: pick the reason that is actually true, not the first one in the list (Chapter 3 explains why the list is kept short enough to make that easy); and write the explanation for someone who was not there — display unit, box damaged, customer shown tells a reviewer everything; customer asked tells them nothing.

Code-based mode. The cashier cannot type a discount at all. Instead:

1. Press Request Discount on the cart header.
2. Search the item, set the quantity, choose percentage or amount, enter the request, and submit.
3. Wait for the approval (Chapter 4 covers what happens in the back office).
4. When approved, press the ticket icon on the line and enter the code you were given.

Rule at the line: a line that already carries a discount code cannot be discounted again. The code is the whole concession for that line.

What cannot be discounted. Five kinds of line refuse discounts, each for a reason:

• Bonus items from a promotion — already free.
• Lines already carrying a promotional discount — the promotion locks the line (Chapter 5).
• Lines carrying a discount code — the code is the concession.
• Gift voucher lines — a voucher always sells at face value.
• Bundle components — the bundle price governs the parts.

The tooltip. When a discount control is greyed out, hover over it: the tooltip states the reason — discounts disabled on the profile, a promotion or code already applied, or no approvers configured. Read it and you can give the customer the real answer instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Markdown reasons
lessons.html:
Approval-based mode depends on the markdown reason list. The list is configured in the back office, and how it is built decides whether the reporting is useful.

Keep the list short and non-overlapping. Five reasons cover most shops: damaged stock, price match, display item, expiring stock, goodwill. Resist the urge to add more. A list of thirty reasons produces useless data: under queue pressure, cashiers pick the first plausible entry, categories blur into each other, and the month-end report answers nothing. The design target is a reason a cashier can pick in two seconds and have it be true — a short list of clearly different reasons achieves that; a long list of precise ones does not.

The budget percentage. Each reason carries a budget percentage — the share of total markdown spend that reason is expected to account for. This turns the markdown report into a comparison of planned against actual, per cause. Examples of what the comparison shows:

• Damaged stock budgeted at 40% of markdowns but running at 70% → a receiving or storage problem, or the reason being used as the easy pick — either way, a specific question to investigate.
• Goodwill budgeted at 10% but running at 40% → a floor habit to look at.
• Price match spiking in one branch → a competitor has moved; useful information arriving through the till.

Set up the reasons before switching the mode on. The rule from the system: in Approval-based mode, if no markdown reasons exist, no discount can be applied at all — the required field has nothing to offer. This is the same pattern as the no-approvers trap in module 2: a control that requires an input becomes a wall when the input was never supplied. Add it to the go-live checklist: before switching a profile to Approval-based, confirm the reasons exist, then process one test discount end to end — reason picked, explanation typed, override cleared.

What the discipline buys. Each discount costs the cashier about thirty seconds of reason-picking and typing. In return, the month-end markdown report can be broken down by cause, branch, cashier and period, against budget. The difference in practice: we discount too much is a feeling nobody can act on; expiring-stock markdowns doubled at the flagship in March, eleven approvals, all one supplier's short-dated deliveries is a specific problem with a specific owner. Chapter 8 shows Okelewo's first quarter of exactly this.

Maintenance. Review the reason list and the budget percentages when the business changes — a new product category, a new competitor, a policy change. The list is small enough to review in ten minutes, which is another argument for keeping it small.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The discount request cycle
lessons.html:
Code-based mode routes every discount through a request-and-approval cycle. This chapter follows one request end to end.

Stage 1 — the request. At the till: Request Discount → search the item → set quantity → choose percentage or amount → enter the ask → submit. The request is now a record in the back office, carrying the item, the quantity, the amount asked, the cashier, the branch, and the time.

Stage 2 — routing. The request is routed to the category leads for that item's group. Approval authority follows the goods, not the location: whoever owns the electronics category's margin answers electronics requests, whichever branch they come from.

Stage 3 — the decision. A category lead reviews the request in the back office and either:

• Approves it — optionally changing the amount (the cashier asked for 15%; the lead grants 10%), or
• Rejects it, with the outcome recorded.

Stage 4 — the code. An approved request produces a discount code, which reaches the cashier.

Stage 5 — application. The cashier enters the code on the line. On entry, the code is reserved briefly against that cashier — so two tills cannot apply the same code at once — then marked used, and stamped on the resulting invoice. A used code cannot be applied again.

Every stage is timestamped with who performed it, so any discount can later be traced from the original request to the final invoice.

Setup requirement: category leads. Item groups must have category leads assigned in the request routing configuration. Without leads, requests have nobody to approve them — the same required-input pattern as approvers (module 2) and markdown reasons (Chapter 3). Before enabling Code-based mode anywhere, confirm every relevant item group has at least one lead, and process one test request end to end.

Where Code-based mode fits. The cycle gives the strongest control available — the decision is made away from counter pressure, by the person who owns the margin, with time to think — at the cost of a round trip: the customer waits, or comes back. That trade suits high-value negotiated goods (electronics, furniture — one request an hour, each worth the wait) and does not suit fast-moving counters (thirty requests a day would stall the queue). Mixed businesses run mixed modes on different profiles: Okelewo's setup (Chapter 8) puts Code-based on the Lagos electronics profile only, with Approval-based everywhere else.

Summary. Request → route to category lead → approve (possibly adjusted) or reject → code → apply once, stamped on the invoice. Leads must exist first. Use the mode where negotiation is normal and volumes are low.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Promotions and bundles
lessons.html:
Promotions and bundles are discounts decided once, centrally, and applied automatically by the till whenever a basket qualifies. Cashiers do not have to remember campaigns, and campaigns cannot be remembered generously.

The three promotion types.

• Product Discount — a percentage or fixed amount off qualifying lines.
• Bonus Item — a free item added to the basket. The bonus line cannot be edited or discounted at the till.
• Bonus Loyalty Points — extra points on a named loyalty programme, optionally with their own validity period.

Setting up a promotion. The fields, in order:

1. Title and description — both are visible to cashiers, so write them for the counter.
2. Valid From / Valid To — outside this window the promotion is ignored, even if its status is Active. Campaigns end by calendar, not by someone remembering to switch them off.
3. Trigger — a specific item, an item group, a brand, or the transaction total.
4. Thresholds — minimum and maximum qualifying quantity (item triggers) or transaction value (basket triggers). Set the maximums: a capped promotion has a known worst-case cost.
5. Reward — the discount type and value, the bonus item, or the points and programme.
6. Automatic or code — the promotion either applies itself when the basket qualifies, or requires a promotion code the cashier enters via the tag icon above the grid. Applied codes appear as removable chips on the cart footer.
7. Status — set Active.

Promotions lock the line. Once a promotional discount lands on a cart line, that line's rate can no longer be edited and no manual discount can be added to it. Reason: the promotion's cost was calculated when the campaign was designed; a manual discount stacked on top would be an unplanned, compounding giveaway. The lock prevents the stack, and the tooltip explains it at the till.

Bundles. A bundle sells a group of items at one price:

• Configuration: a main item, a bundle price, and the component items with quantities.
• At the till: adding the main item where a bundle exists offers the choice — bundle or single item. Choosing the bundle brings the components in as indented child lines under the main line.
• Child lines have fixed quantity, rate and discount — the bundle price governs the parts. To remove a bundle, remove its main line.

Retiring a bundle. Set it inactive rather than deleting it. Deleting loses the component list; an inactive bundle can be reactivated next season with its configuration intact.

Practical rule. Wherever a regular, repeated discount exists on the floor — the seasonal offer, the multi-buy, the staple combo — convert it into a promotion or bundle. Every giveaway moved from floor habit into a configured campaign gains a validity window, a cost cap, and a report line.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Rate edits, credit releases, and the approval mechanics
lessons.html:
Two powers go beyond ordinary discounting, and both run through the Power Approver machinery. This chapter covers the powers, then the machinery itself in detail.

Rate edits. Where the profile allows it, the pencil icon on a line opens Edit Rate, and the unit price itself can be overwritten. Facts:

• A rate edit is stronger than a discount: a discount is limited by the price, a rate edit replaces the price.
• Every edited line is marked Rate override, permanently visible on review.
• Where Require Override for Rate Edit is on (module 2 recommended it wherever rate editing is allowed), an approver clears every change.

Supervision note: rate-edit frequency per cashier is worth checking weekly. A till whose sales regularly carry Rate override markers has prices being set by memory — the exact habit the price list exists to end. Okelewo hits this in Chapter 8.

Credit limit releases. When a customer is over their limit, the cart shows Sales suspended due to customer outstanding and payment is blocked. An approver holding the Credit Limit Override permission can release the sale. Treat the release as what it is: a decision to extend the business's exposure beyond the recorded limit, made on the approver's name, for this sale. If the same customer needs releasing week after week, the limit itself needs a decision — raise it formally or hold it — rather than repeated releases by momentum.

The approval mechanics. Wherever an approval is required — discounts, returns, cart clearing, rate edits, credit releases — it works one of two ways, per the profile's override mode:

• Password. The approver enters their email and password at the till. Fast, works offline, requires the approver physically present.
• One-time code. The till requests a code. A six-digit code is emailed to every approver holding the relevant permission; any of them can read it to the cashier over the phone. The code expires after one hour, and the terminal must be online to request one.

Troubleshooting a code that never arrives — three causes, in order:

1. The approver's account has no email address (or a wrong one).
2. The terminal was offline when the request was made.
3. The code is past its hour — request a fresh one.

A useful property of the code design. Because every code request is emailed to all holders of that permission, no override can be quietly arranged between one cashier and one obliging approver — the whole approver group sees every request. And because every completed approval records who approved what and when, approvals can be counted by approver: an approver whose password clears forty discounts a week is either genuinely the floor's only available approver (a staffing problem) or approving without looking (a supervision problem). The count is how you tell which. Module 8 puts this check on the weekly routine.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The Return & Exchange console
lessons.html:
The Return & Exchange console appears in the sidebar when the profile enables at least one of: cash refund, exchange, or the return policy (module 2). A return runs in three steps.

Step 1 — Find Invoice. Scan the receipt barcode, or type the reference — either the till reference or the back-office invoice number works (offline sales can be found by their local reference too). Multiple matches offer a choice. The invoice summary then shows: date, outstanding amount, item count, and whether the sale is still inside the return window.

Rule: no invoice, no return. There is no path through this console that starts from nothing — which is the wall in front of the phantom-return fraud from module 1. And read the window flag now: it tells you immediately whether this return is routine or will need the beyond-window override, before the conversation goes further.

Step 2 — Build Return. Two forms:

• Refund. Select the lines and quantities coming back. Choose a reason from the list: defective item, wrong item delivered, customer changed mind, damaged in transit, quality issues, size or colour issue, other. Then choose where the money goes: Store Credit, or Cash Refund — cash appears only if the profile permits it.
• Exchange. As above, plus search and add the replacement goods. The difference is calculated in both directions: if the customer owes more, choose a payment method for the balance; if the customer is owed, choose the refund method.

Serial-numbered items: the console asks which serials are coming back. The unit returned must be the unit sold — the same link that was created at the sale, checked in reverse.

Step 3 — Complete. Where the profile requires it, an approver authorises the return (password or code, per the return override mode). The return posts, and a return or exchange receipt prints.

Loyalty recovery. If the original sale earned loyalty points that have since been spent, the system calculates the amount to recover and adds it to what the customer owes, showing the figure before completion. Why: refunding the goods while ignoring the spent points would pay the customer twice — once in the refund, once in the points already redeemed. Read the figure from the screen to the customer; it is the system's calculation, not your estimate.

Returns need the connection. The Return & Exchange console is unavailable while the terminal is offline — the original invoice, the loyalty ledger and the balances all live on the server. During an outage, take the customer's details or ask them to return when the connection is back.

Summary of the safeguards. Find the invoice first; a reason on every return; cash only where the profile allows; an approver where required; serials checked in reverse; spent points recovered; and the whole flow online-only. Each safeguard is one of the five parts from Chapter 1, built into the screens.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: Okelewo's first quarter of exceptions
lessons.html:
Ninety days after go-live, the discount and returns data comes up for its first serious review. Four findings and two events, each tied to a chapter.

Finding 1 — expiring stock over budget (Chapter 3). Expiring-stock markdowns run at double their budget percentage at the flagship. Breaking the figure down takes twenty minutes: eleven approvals, all in provisions, all traceable to one supplier's short-dated deliveries. The finding goes to purchasing with the report attached — a supplier conversation, not a counter problem. This is the budget comparison doing its job: the number pointed at a cause.

Finding 2 — thin explanations (Chapter 2). Goodwill markdowns are under budget everywhere except one Lagos cashier, whose explanations read customer asked three times in a month. Because the explanations exist, the review is a five-minute coaching conversation about writing useful ones — not an accusation, and not a mystery.

Finding 3 — price match spike (Chapter 3). Price-match markdowns spike in Abeokuta the same week a competitor opens nearby. Nothing to fix — but the till has just delivered competitive intelligence with dates on it.

Finding 4 — the Friday rate edits (Chapter 6). The weekly rate-override check shows one flagship till repeatedly carrying Rate override markers on Fridays. The cause: a senior cashier matching prices from memory for regular customers. The response: Require Override for Rate Edit is switched on for that profile the same week. The marker did its job — the habit was visible, and the fix was one checkbox.

Event 1 — the Code-based pilot (Chapter 4). The Lagos electronics section goes Code-based. Setup order followed: the category lead assigned first, one test request processed end to end, then the mode switched. First month's cycle data: nineteen requests; fourteen approved, six of them with the amount adjusted down by the lead; five rejected with outcomes recorded. One attempted reuse of a morning's code in the afternoon is refused — used codes stay used — and becomes a training note.

Event 2 — the first hard returns (Chapter 7). Three firsts at the returns desk: the first beyond-window return (day 34, a defective kettle) — the window flag shows at Find Invoice, the supervisor's override clears it, the reason is on record; the first loyalty recovery — the spent points appear in the amount owed before completion, the cashier reads the figure from the screen, and there is no argument because the number is the system's; and the ninety-day cash refund decision, scheduled at go-live, comes due — the quarter's returns volumes are low and clean, so cash refunds are enabled at the flagship only, with the override required, while store credit remains the default elsewhere. The conservative launch setting is relaxed on evidence, on schedule.

The MD's quarter note: we gave away less, argued less, and I can see where every conceded naira went.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & module rule 5
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

The five parts (Chapter 1). Every exception records: what, who asked, who approved, why, and the record itself. A missing part — the discount with no reason, the return with no invoice, the override with no approver — is the finding.

The modes at the till (Chapter 2). Standard: direct entry, percentage capped at 100, amount capped at the rate, override at the moment where required. Approval-based: reason plus typed explanation, neither blank, stored on the line; pick the true reason and write for someone who was not there. Code-based: no typed discounts — request, wait, apply the code; a coded line cannot be discounted again. Cannot be discounted: bonus items, promoted lines, coded lines, voucher lines, bundle components. Hover the greyed control for the reason.

Markdown reasons (Chapter 3). Five short, non-overlapping reasons beat thirty precise ones. Budget percentages turn the report into planned-versus-actual per cause. In Approval-based mode with no reasons configured, no discount can be applied at all — reasons first, then the mode, then one test discount.

The request cycle (Chapter 4). Request → routed to the item group's category leads → approved (amount adjustable) or rejected → code → applied once, reserved against the cashier, marked used, stamped on the invoice. Every stage timestamped. Leads must exist before the mode goes live. Fits low-volume negotiated goods.

Promotions and bundles (Chapter 5). Three types: product discount, bonus item, bonus points. Outside the validity window a promotion is ignored even if Active. Set the maximum thresholds. A promotional discount locks its line against further edits. Bundles: main item, bundle price, fixed child lines; retire by setting inactive, never deleting.

The stronger powers (Chapter 6). A rate edit replaces the price and is always marked Rate override; require the override wherever it is allowed; check the markers per cashier weekly. A credit release extends exposure on the approver's name; a customer released weekly needs a limit decision instead. Approval mechanics: password (fast, offline, present) or one-time code (six digits, emailed to every holder, one hour, online to request). Code not arriving: no email, offline request, or expired. Count approvals by approver monthly.

Returns (Chapter 7). Find Invoice first — no invoice, no return; the summary shows the window status. Build: refund (reason from the fixed list; store credit, or cash only where permitted) or exchange (difference both ways); serials asked in reverse. Complete: approver where required. Loyalty recovery is calculated and shown before completion. The console is unavailable offline.

The quarter (Chapter 8). Budget comparisons pointed at a supplier; explanations enabled coaching; markers exposed the Friday habit; the pilot's leads-first order; the beyond-window override; cash refunds relaxed on evidence at ninety days.

Module rule 5: every discount and every return carries a reason and an approver. Module 6 covers Lay-By, Staff Purchase, Airtime and the Customer Desk.

extended_counters.title: POS 6 — Extended Counter Operations
extended_counters.desc: The extended counters as financial arrangements: creating and managing lay-bys through completion or manager-gated termination, staff purchases with the payroll recovery chain proven end to end, airtime under the consumed-on-issue rule with reprint-by-invoice, Sales History and the Customer Desk with the reversible monthly merge, and Inventory Ops with prioritised requests, confirmed-quantity receiving, offline label printing and the Message Hub.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The extended counters
lessons.html:
Beyond the Sales Console, the sidebar carries a set of consoles that look like customer services: Lay-By, Staff Purchase, Airtime Sales, Sales History, Customer Desk, and Inventory Ops. This module covers each one. The module rule: every extended counter is a financial arrangement, and each is run with the controls its money deserves.

What each console really handles. Look past the service and name the money:

• Lay-By holds a customer's deposit against reserved goods. The business is holding the customer's money (owed back if the arrangement fails) and the customer's goods (out of the sellable pool). Two exposures in one arrangement.
• Staff Purchase is employee credit — the business lending against future wages, with a limit, a running balance, and repayment through payroll.
• Airtime is prepaid stock whose entire value is a code. It is the closest thing the counter sells to cash itself.
• Customer Desk is the customer's financial record — balances, invoices and payments per person.
• Inventory Ops is stock moving between locations — requests, transfers, and the receiving check.

Why the naming matters. These counters are exactly where informal shops leak: the lay-by book nobody reconciles, staff purchases sorted out at month end, an airtime float that is about right, a customer file with four spellings of one person. Each of those is a money control skipped because the arrangement looked like a service. ZhiftPOS builds the controls in — deposits computed and taken, limits enforced, codes counted, records merged — and this module shows how each works and what to check.

Module contents. Chapter 2: creating a lay-by. Chapter 3: managing lay-bys through to completion or termination. Chapter 4: staff purchases and the payroll connection. Chapter 5: airtime sales and the consumed-on-issue rule. Chapter 6: Sales History and the Customer Desk, including duplicate merging. Chapter 7: Inventory Ops, Label Printing and the Message Hub. Chapter 8: Okelewo's rollout of all of them. Chapter 9: review.

One connection to note now. Everything these consoles do posts into the same system as ordinary sales: lay-by instalments appear in the shift close, staff purchase balances sit in a real account and are recovered through payroll, airtime is stocked and counted like inventory, and transfers move real stock. There are no side books; every arrangement lives in the standard records.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Creating a lay-by
lessons.html:
A lay-by reserves goods against a deposit, with the balance paid over scheduled instalments. Creating one properly takes four steps and four habits.

Procedure.

1. Add the items the customer is reserving, exactly as in a normal sale — including batch and serial entry where the goods are tracked. Reserved goods are still tracked goods.
2. Identify the customer by phone number. A lay-by is never anonymous: the arrangement will need follow-up, and the phone number is how the follow-up happens. Read the number back or ring it once at entry.
3. Review the total and the deposit. The required deposit is computed from the profile's Lay-By Deposit % (module 2). At Okelewo this is 15%.
4. Take the deposit. On payment, the instalment schedule is created from the profile's instalment count and day spacing.

The schedule. Each instalment carries: due date, amount due, amount paid, balance, and status — unpaid, partly paid, paid, or overdue. The schedule is, in effect, a small receivables ledger for this one arrangement, and the statuses are what Chapter 3's management works from.

Four habits that prevent the classic lay-by problems.

• Take the deposit before setting anything aside. A lay-by without its deposit is a free reservation — the customer risks nothing, and abandoned arrangements pile up. The profile computes the minimum; collect it at creation, always.
• Print and explain the schedule. The customer should leave holding the dates and amounts. A payment reminder weeks later should be a reminder, not a surprise.
• Physically separate reserved goods. A lay-by shelf, away from the sales floor. A reserved item left on the shelf gets sold on a busy Saturday, and the business then owes a customer goods it no longer has.
• Verify the phone number at entry. Everything in Chapter 3 — the overdue call, the termination notice — depends on the number being real.

Decide the forfeiture policy before the first dispute. What happens to the deposit if the customer abandons the lay-by? Whatever the answer, decide it as policy, print it on the schedule, and say it at creation. A forfeiture rule announced at the start generates no argument later; one invented during a dispute generates nothing else. (Okelewo's version, and how it played out, is in Chapter 8.)

Summary. Items in, phone verified, deposit computed and taken, schedule created, printed and explained, goods physically set aside, forfeiture terms known. A lay-by created this way is easy to manage; every shortcut here becomes a problem in Chapter 3.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Managing lay-bys
lessons.html:
Every lay-by ends one of two ways — completed or terminated. The console manages both, and the long middle between.

The Open Lay-Bys panel. All outstanding lay-bys, each with its schedule and statuses. Read it as an ageing list: the overdue instalments are the work. Check the panel weekly (it is on module 8's calendar), and follow up overdue instalments by phone from the recorded number. A lay-by left silent for months becomes the classic mess: goods held for someone unreachable, a deposit nobody can match to a person, and stock in limbo.

Taking an instalment: Make Payment.

1. Open the lay-by and choose Make Payment.
2. Enter the amount and choose the payment method.
3. The schedule updates — instalments move to paid or partly paid.

Notes: payments in any workable pattern are fine — two instalments at once, or half of one; that is what partly paid exists for. Each payment lands on its payment method and is included in the shift close — lay-by activity is summarised in the Close Shift window, so these takings are counted with everything else. Print the updated schedule for the customer each time.

Completion. When the final instalment is paid, the goods are released to the customer. The reservation becomes a completed sale, and the shelf clears.

Termination. Terminate cancels the lay-by. The procedure has controls built in:

1. Choose Terminate on the lay-by.
2. Select the refund method for what the customer has paid (subject to the forfeiture policy, and routed like any refund — store credit where cash refunds are off).
3. A manager's email and password are required. Termination is always an authorised event: money is going backwards and goods are being released from a customer arrangement, and cancelling-and-pocketing is the lay-by's classic fraud. The manager step is the control.
4. On completion, the goods return to stock — the reservation is released and the inventory is correct again.

The terminated lay-by's record survives: who reserved, what was paid, who authorised the end. Nothing about a termination is deleted.

The three numbers a healthy lay-by book shows. At any moment, the console should be able to answer: total deposits and instalments held, total balances still due, and which goods are reserved. All three reconcile against reality — the money against the accounts, the goods against the lay-by shelf. Module 8's routines include exactly that check.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Staff purchases
lessons.html:
Staff Purchase lets employees buy at a staff discount and repay through payroll. It is employee credit with the controls built in — a limit, a visible balance, automatic recovery — and this chapter covers the flow and the setup that makes it real.

The purchase, step by step.

1. Open the Staff Purchase console and enter the employee identifier.
2. The screen shows the employee's credit position: purchase limit, current exposure, remaining balance, and estimated monthly repayment. The employee sees their own position before anything is added.
3. Add the items. The staff discount applies automatically to every line — the percentage from the profile (which takes precedence over any company-wide staff discount at this counter).
4. Complete. Two things happen: the purchase is booked to the employee purchase account, and it is scheduled for recovery through payroll.

The hard limit. A purchase that would take the employee past their limit is refused. There is no override at the till, by design: the limit is set on the employee's record by whoever manages employment terms, and that is where any exception belongs. The refusal is rarely contested in practice, because the screen showed the arithmetic before the attempt.

The wiring that must exist. Three records make the feature work end to end — confirm all three before enabling it:

1. A purchase limit on each participating employee's record.
2. The employee purchase account named in the company-wide settings — where outstanding balances sit, visible to finance per person.
3. The salary component named in the company-wide settings — the payroll deduction that recovers the balances.

Then prove the chain once: one real purchase, through the account, into a payroll run, recovered by the component. A half-wired setup — purchases booking but recovery never configured — is an interest-free loan book growing quietly under a staff-benefit label. The one-time test prevents it.

The Open Staff Purchases panel. Lists outstanding balances, searchable by staff name or reference, each showing total and remaining balance. Review it on the same weekly rhythm as the lay-by panel.

Take Payment. Records a direct repayment outside payroll — an employee clearing some or all of a balance in cash before the payroll run. The payment lands on its method, the exposure reduces, and the payroll recovery adjusts to the remainder.

Summary. Identifier → position shown → discount automatic → limit enforced with no till override → booked to the account → recovered by payroll (or by Take Payment). Wire all three records and test the chain before the first purchase.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Airtime sales
lessons.html:
The Airtime console sells mobile recharge vouchers. The product is a code: reveal it and it is spent. That one fact drives every rule in this chapter.

The sale, in three steps.

1. Select Carrier — choose the network.
2. Choose Amount — pick a denomination and set the quantity. Availability is shown, and the sale is capped at what is in stock: airtime is inventory, and the console will not sell codes it does not hold.
3. Complete Payment — choose the method and finish.

Each voucher then prints on its own slip with its recharge code — one slip per code.

The consumed-on-issue rule. Memorise this: an airtime code is consumed the moment it is issued. When the sale completes, that code is revealed from stock and is spent — whether or not the paper reached the customer's hand. Two instructions follow:

• Print before the customer leaves. The slip is the product.
• If the printer fails, reprint from the invoice — never sell again. Vouchers can be reprinted by looking up the invoice number: the same code is recovered, on the same sale, with no second consumption. Ringing a new sale instead consumes a second code against one payment — one code in the customer's hand, one lost (or worse, in a pocket). The reflex to train: printer fails → note the invoice number → reprint. Never resell.

Airtime as stock. Treat the codes like the inventory they are:

• The availability display is the stock count — watch it, and reorder from the sales figures before running out. (At Okelewo, recharge vouchers turned out to be the flagship's top-selling item — an airtime stockout there is a revenue event.)
• The reconciliation is simple arithmetic: codes received − codes issued = codes held. It is as countable as the cash drawer, and it goes on the same routine: a count that does not reconcile has a story that needs finding.

Reprints and disputes. Any airtime voucher can be reprinted from its invoice. A customer returning with a code they say did not work is handled from the record: the invoice shows the code that was issued, when, and on which sale — the conversation starts from facts, not memory.

Summary. Carrier → amount and quantity (stock-capped) → payment → one slip per code. The code is consumed at issue: print before the customer leaves, reprint by invoice on failure, never resell. Count received − issued = held on the regular routine.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Sales History and the Customer Desk
lessons.html:
Two lookup consoles turn the counter's records into answers: Sales History for transactions, the Customer Desk for people.

Sales History. Recent transactions, with tools to find any of them:

• Filter by date range; search by reference or customer name; narrow to voucher activity, a single cashier, or a single shift.
• Returns are marked with a Return label, so they are never mistaken for sales.
• Any entry opens to its lines and recorded payments, and the receipt can be reprinted from there.

The everyday use case — the lost receipt: search by the customer's name, or any fragment of the reference. Offline sales are found by their local reference just as posted sales are found by their invoice number. A lost receipt is a one-minute lookup, not a dead end.

Note for supervisors: the cashier and shift filters make this console the starting point for reviewing any specific person or period — module 8 uses them.

The Customer Desk. One customer's full picture, in three views:

• Details — contact information, price list, credit limit, payment terms and loyalty points, plus the statistics: outstanding balance, total invoiced, total paid, total orders, average order value, purchase frequency, last purchase, and return rate. Read the return rate: a customer returning a third of what they buy is a pattern worth understanding, whatever the explanation turns out to be.
• Invoices — everything bought, filterable by status and date, searchable by number, printable.
• Payments — receipts with reference, date and amount.

Edit Customer updates the name, mobile, email and loyalty card from the same screen.

Duplicate customers and merging. Two protections keep one person as one record:

• Automatic merge at creation (on by default): a new customer whose mobile number matches an existing record merges into it immediately. Leave this on unless customers genuinely share phone numbers.
• The merge tool, for duplicates that slip through: it scans for customers sharing a mobile or email, you choose the surviving record, and the history merges into it. The merge is reversible — a snapshot is kept, and cancelling the merge restores both records.

Run the duplicate scan monthly. The practical reason: loyalty depends on it. A customer split across two records has their points split too — half their history on each — and they will notice. The desk's statistics also assume one person per record; duplicates quietly corrupt every figure on the Details view.

Summary. Sales History: filter, search, Return labels, reprints — the lost receipt answered in a minute. Customer Desk: details with statistics (watch the return rate), invoices, payments, edit. Duplicates: mobile-match auto-merge at creation, the reversible merge tool monthly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Inventory Ops, Label Printing, and the Message Hub
lessons.html:
Three consoles connect the counter to stock: what is held, what is requested, what is moving — plus the labels for the shelf and the hub that carries the traffic.

The Inventory tab. Stock as this terminal knows it:

• Filter by warehouse (where the profile permits viewing other warehouses — the is-it-at-the-other-branch question answered from the chair), by item group, or by free search on code, name or brand.
• Counters summarise items in stock, low on stock, and out of stock.
• A synchronising marker appears while figures refresh — the number on screen is the local copy's number, and the marker shows when it is being updated.

Material Requests — asking another location for stock.

1. Choose New Request. Confirm the requesting warehouse and select the source warehouse.
2. Set a priority: low, medium, high or urgent.
3. Add each item and quantity, plus a note explaining what is needed and why.
4. Submit.

Both directions are visible: requests you have raised and requests raised against your branch, each opening to its full item list and status. The request replaces the phone call and the chat message with a document the other branch can act on and everyone can see.

Stock Transfers — goods actually moving. A transfer is raised at the sending side and received at yours. The receiving rule is the one to memorise: confirm the quantities as you accept them. If twelve were sent and eleven arrived, record eleven. A short delivery confirmed at receiving creates the discrepancy record at the boundary between branches, where it can be investigated cheaply. A short delivery waved through at the paper quantity disappears into your branch's stock figures and resurfaces months later as an unexplainable count variance. Ten seconds of counting at the door, or a mystery in December — that is the trade.

Label Printing. Shelf and product labels, printed from the till:

• Add items singly by search, or in bulk — an entire item group, or all the lines from a goods receipt or stock entry (a new delivery labelled without retyping).
• Set the label count per row, choose the template (module 3's proven presets), preview, print.
• Works offline — the shelf can be priced through an outage.

The Message Hub. The counter's inbox: notices, transfer alerts and requests, filed like mail — unread, starred, transfers, requests, system, alerts, archived — searchable, with important notices pinned and the unread count on the top-bar envelope. The operational point: transfer and request messages carry their underlying details and can be acted on directly from the hub. Keep the counter's operational traffic here, in one visible stream, rather than scattered across personal phones.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: Okelewo's extended counters
lessons.html:
Okelewo enables the extended counters in its second quarter, demand first. The events worth learning from:

Lay-by (Chapters 2-3). Launched first — customers had been asking, especially for big-ticket items. The creation habits hold from day one: 15% deposits taken at creation, schedules printed and explained, a lay-by shelf established behind the flagship counter, phone numbers read back at entry. The forfeiture policy is decided before launch and printed on every schedule.

The test arrives on schedule: one lay-by goes two instalments overdue. The weekly panel check flags it; two calls to the recorded number go unanswered; the termination runs by the book — manager credentials at the gate, the refundable portion routed to store credit (cash refunds are still off), the goods back to stock the same hour, the record intact. The retained portion follows the printed policy, and there is no argument, because the schedule said what the schedule said from the day it was created.

Staff purchase (Chapter 4). Enabled at the flagship only, and only after the full-chain test: one real purchase, through the employee purchase account, into a payroll run, recovered by the salary component — proven before the second employee bought anything. The quarter stays uneventful: limits visible to their holders, one over-limit attempt refused without argument (the screen had shown the arithmetic), one Take Payment repayment ahead of payroll, and finance reading the account per person at month end. The old informal habit — staff goods sorted out at month end from memory — simply stops, because the ledger replaced it.

Airtime (Chapter 5). The surprise of the quarter: recharge vouchers are the flagship's top-selling item — six hundred units of one denomination in a month. Airtime stock is promoted to a managed float: availability checked daily, reorders triggered from the sales report. The consumed-on-issue drill pays off in week nine: a printer jams mid-sale, and the cashier's trained reflex runs — invoice number noted, slip reprinted, same code recovered. The untrained response (ring it again) would have consumed a second code against one payment. The received − issued = held count joins the daily routine and reconciles all quarter.

The record consoles (Chapter 6). A lost-receipt customer is served in ninety seconds from Sales History — name search, an offline-era local reference found, receipt reprinted. The Customer Desk's return-rate figure flags one account at 31%; investigation finds a genuine cause — a sizing problem in one product line — which goes to purchasing as buying feedback. The figure was worth reading either way. The first monthly duplicate scan finds nine pairs; they are merged with survivors chosen — and one merge is reversed the next day when a shared family phone number comes to light. The snapshot restores both records exactly as promised.

Receiving (Chapter 7). The first short delivery is caught at the flagship door: twelve sent from the Distribution Centre, eleven received, eleven confirmed. The discrepancy record points the investigation at the sending warehouse, where a pick error is found within the week. Under the old routine, the missing unit would have dissolved into the flagship's stock figures and reappeared in December as unexplained shrinkage.

The MD's quarter note: the side counters turned out to be money wearing disguises. We run them with the same controls now, and the month-end sorting-out meetings have nothing left to sort.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & module rule 6
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

The consoles named (Chapter 1). Lay-By = a deposit held against reserved goods (two exposures). Staff Purchase = employee credit recovered through payroll. Airtime = prepaid stock whose value is the code. Customer Desk = the customer's financial record. Inventory Ops = stock in motion. No side books — everything posts into the same system.

Creating a lay-by (Chapter 2). Items (with batches/serials), customer by verified phone number, deposit computed from the profile percentage and taken, schedule created from the count and spacing. Print and explain the schedule; separate the goods physically; decide and print the forfeiture policy before the first dispute. Each instalment: due date, amounts, balance, status (unpaid / partly paid / paid / overdue).

Managing lay-bys (Chapter 3). Check the Open Lay-Bys panel weekly; the overdue lines are the work. Make Payment updates the schedule, lands on its method, and is included in the shift close. Completion releases the goods. Termination requires a manager's email and password, routes the refund per policy, returns the goods to stock, and keeps the full record.

Staff purchases (Chapter 4). The screen shows limit, exposure, remaining balance and estimated repayment before anything is added. The discount applies automatically. Over-limit purchases are refused with no till override — the exception belongs with the employee record's owner. Wiring: the employee limit, the purchase account, the salary component — and one full-chain test before launch. Take Payment records direct repayment outside payroll.

Airtime (Chapter 5). Carrier → denomination and quantity (capped at stock) → payment → one slip per code. The code is consumed the moment it is issued: print before the customer leaves; on printer failure, reprint from the invoice number — never sell again. Count: received − issued = held.

The record consoles (Chapter 6). Sales History: filters by date, reference, customer, voucher, cashier, shift; Return labels; reprints; the lost receipt found by either reference. Customer Desk: details with statistics (watch the return rate), invoices, payments, edit. Duplicates: mobile-match auto-merge at creation; the monthly merge tool, reversible by snapshot; loyalty depends on one person, one record.

Stock consoles (Chapter 7). Inventory tab: warehouse filter where permitted, the three stock counters, the synchronising marker. Material requests: source, priority, items, note — both directions visible. Transfers: confirm quantities at receiving — record the short at the boundary instead of absorbing it. Label Printing: bulk from a goods receipt, works offline. Message Hub: one stream, actionable transfer and request messages.

The quarter (Chapter 8). The printed forfeiture policy ending arguments before they start; the full-chain staff purchase test; the printer-jam reprint reflex; the 31% return rate that turned out to be buying feedback; the reversed merge; the short delivery caught at the door.

Module rule 6: every extended counter is a financial arrangement, run with the controls its money deserves. Module 7 covers the gift voucher programme end to end.
