voucher_programme.title: POS 7 — The Voucher Programme
voucher_programme.desc: The gift voucher programme end to end: the Voucher Console and its roles, sellable versus complimentary cards with the activation gate and six states, the accounts wired before the first card, design/generate/import, activation with the approver record and the two printing rules, the counter's two selling routes with the daily till-batch check, the register and the permanent void, the four accounting events with breakage as a deliberate finance decision, the monthly check, and the seven watch-points.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The voucher programme and the console
lessons.html:
Module 2 configured the voucher settings on the profile; module 4 covered selling a voucher at the till. This module covers running the programme itself, using the Voucher Console — the full-screen workspace, reached at the site's /vouchers address, that keeps a complete record of every card from creation to final redemption. The module rule: a voucher is money the business owes, tracked from creation to expiry.

What a voucher is. A voucher is a promise of value: a card worth 5,000 can be spent by whoever holds it, in your stores. From the moment a card is sold, that value is money the business owes — and it stays owed until the card is spent or expires. Everything in this module follows from that: the accounting rules (Chapter 3), the activation control on free cards (Chapter 2), the printing rules (Chapter 5), and the checks (Chapter 8).

The roles. Access to the console is role-based:

• Voucher Manager — everything in the console: create, import, activate, print, browse and cancel cards, and edit the Setup and Design screens. At Okelewo this is the accountant.
• Administrator — everything, plus accounts, roles and system-wide settings.
• Accounts Manager — the accounts the programme posts to, and the recognition of lapsed value as income (Chapter 7).
• Counter staff — sell and redeem at the till with ordinary till permissions. They work in the till, not the console.

Note the separation: the person who creates voucher value, the people who handle it at counters, and the person who accounts for it are different capabilities, assigned separately. Keep them separate — Chapter 8 explains what goes wrong when one person holds all three.

The console's sections. The left-hand rail:

• Overview — the whole programme at a glance (Chapter 6).
• Batches — every batch of cards; open one to activate or print.
• Vouchers — the searchable register of every individual card.
• Generate — create a new batch.
• Import — bring pre-printed card stock into the system.
• Design — the printed card's appearance, per company.
• Setup — the accounts the programme posts to, per company.

Setup and Design are configured once per company and rarely touched again. The other five are the everyday programme. The module covers them in the order value moves: accounts first (Chapter 3 — nothing should be created before the books are wired), then design and creation (4), activation and printing (5), the counter and the register (6), the accounting and the monthly check (7), and what to watch (8).

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Card types, card states, and the activation gate
lessons.html:
The two kinds. Every card is one of:

• Sellable — a gift card a customer buys. Its validity clock starts at the sale: valid for the configured number of days from the day it is bought. Sellable cards are created ready to sell.
• Complimentary — a card given away free: a prize, an apology, a promotion. Complimentary cards are created inactive and cannot be used until a manager activates them. Their validity clock starts at activation.

Why the activation gate exists. No money changes hands when complimentary cards are created, so a batch of them is, until activated, a box of potential money that cost nothing to make. The gate means: a stolen or prematurely released batch cannot be redeemed — the cards are worthless until someone with authority switches them on. Creating cards (generating or importing) therefore never creates spendable value by itself; a second, recorded act by an authorised person does. Assign that authority deliberately — it belongs to the Voucher Manager, not to whoever happens to print.

The six states. Every card is always in exactly one state:

• Available — live stock: a sellable card ready to sell, or a complimentary card not yet activated.
• Sold — issued and carrying its full value (bought at a till, or activated as complimentary).
• Partially redeemed — some value spent; a balance remains.
• Redeemed — fully spent.
• Expired — the validity period ended with value still on the card (Chapter 7 covers what happens to that value).
• Void — cancelled by a manager. A void card can never be redeemed. Cancellation is permanent; a card voided in error is replaced by creating or importing another, and the cancellation itself stays on the record.

Two constants per card. Whatever the state:

• The balance — starts at face value, falls as the card is spent.
• The serial number — the card's permanent reference, printed on the card and shown in the console. Every search, dispute and history lookup resolves to it.

Summary. Sellable cards: ready at creation, clock from sale. Complimentary cards: inactive at creation, activated by a manager, clock from activation. Six states from Available to Void; a void is final and stays on record; the balance and serial identify every card for life. Chapter 3 wires the accounts these cards will post to; Chapter 5 operates the activation gate described here.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Setup: the accounts
lessons.html:
Because a sold voucher is money owed, the sale has to post to the right accounts. The Setup screen configures this once per company — before the first card is created.

The two accounts.

• Liability account. When a customer buys a gift card, the cash comes in and this account records what the business now owes. It must be a liability-type account belonging to the company. Every voucher sale credits it.
• Promotional expense account (optional). Where the cost of complimentary cards is recorded when they are redeemed. If left blank, complimentary redemptions fall back to the liability account — it works, but the books are clearer with the expense account named.

Two ways to complete Setup.

1. Choose your own accounts from the company's chart. The console validates each choice on four points: it belongs to the right company, it is the right kind of account, it is a real posting account (not a group heading), and it is active. Pass all four and the console wires the rest automatically.
2. Create defaults for me. One click creates a suitable liability account, an expense account, the voucher product, its tax treatment, and the till payment method — everything listed on screen for later adjustment.

Either way, a status banner then confirms the company is ready to issue vouchers and names its liability account. (A company that never opens Setup still works on system-standard accounts — Setup makes the books readable, it is not what makes vouchers function.)

The accounting rule behind it. Understand this once and Chapter 7 is easy: selling a voucher is not a sale — it is a promise. The customer has paid, but no goods have been handed over. So:

• The money received is recorded as a liability — value owed — never as revenue.
• No sales tax is charged on the voucher sale. Tax belongs on the goods, and the goods have not been bought yet.
• Revenue and tax are recognised later, at redemption, on the goods the customer actually takes.

Why getting this wrong matters. A business that books voucher sales as revenue makes four errors at once: the selling month is overstated, the redemption month is understated, tax is charged at the wrong time, and the outstanding-liability figure — what the business actually owes cardholders — disappears from the books. A strong December voucher push raises cash and raises debt in equal measure; the revenue arrives in January when the cards come back. Okelewo's MD summarised it correctly in Chapter 8: a voucher programme is a loan from customers who intend to spend it with you.

Order of operations. Setup first, then Design, then the first batch. Nothing is minted into unwired books.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Design, Generate, and Import
lessons.html:
Design. Every printed card has two halves: the left half is the branded panel — logo, colours and wording, configured per company — and the right half is a standard information panel identical on every card: usage notes, the barcode, the written code, the serial number and the validity. Two ways to design the branded half:

• Guided design. Upload a logo (optionally a strip of feature icons), pick background, highlight and text colours, write two short taglines (one for gift cards, one for complimentary), and add footer lines — website, email, social. The console lays it out.
• Custom design. Supply your own artwork and layout; the console inserts each card's live details — amount, company name, the correct tagline, footers — so one design serves every value and both kinds.

Two useful facts: the live preview is drawn by the same engine that does the real printing, so what you see is genuinely what prints; and a company with no saved design prints on a clean neutral panel built from its name — you can start selling immediately and design later.

Generate — creating a new batch. Five choices:

1. Type — Complimentary (created inactive) or Sellable (created ready).
2. Company.
3. Value — a preset or any typed amount. Every card in a batch carries the same value; a batch is one denomination, which keeps counting and reporting simple.
4. Quantity — up to 10,000 cards per batch.
5. Validity — days usable, counted from sale (sellable) or activation (complimentary).

Press Generate: the console creates the batch and assigns every card a unique code and serial number, then opens the batch — sellable batches ready to print and sell, complimentary batches waiting for activation.

Import — bringing pre-printed stock in. For physical cards that already exist (for example older stock with printed serials):

1. Enter company, value and validity, as with Generate.
2. Enter the serials: pasted one per line, comma-separated, or as a range — 0001-0500 imports five hundred. The screen confirms how many it found.
3. Review the preview and confirm.

Two rules about imported cards:

• The number already printed on each card stays the code used to redeem it. Cards in circulation keep working unchanged.
• Imported cards arrive as an inactive complimentary batch and must be activated like any other. Legacy stock is a box of potential money exactly like a fresh batch, so the same gate applies.

Summary. Design once per company (guided or custom; the preview is faithful; the fallback is neutral). Generate by type, company, one value per batch, up to 10,000, with validity set at creation. Import by pasted serials or ranges; printed numbers remain the codes; imports arrive inactive.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Activation and printing
lessons.html:
Activating a complimentary batch.

1. Open the batch from Batches (or from the link shown right after generating or importing).
2. Select the cards to issue — select all, or tick individual rows. Partial activation is a normal choice: activate 120 of a 500-card batch for this month's campaign and leave the rest as inert stock.
3. Optionally record each card's issued-to and reason. These notes stay on the card's record and are printed on the card itself — a complimentary card that names its recipient and purpose is easy to question if it turns up anywhere else.
4. Press Activate. The system records you as the approver, sets the issue and expiry dates, and moves the cards to the Sold (issued) state. Only now can they be printed and redeemed.

Keep the gate meaningful: activation authority sits with the Voucher Manager, activations should match planned campaigns, and the approver stamp means every activation has a name on it. Chapter 8 includes the check that uses this.

Printing. With a batch open, select the cards and press Print. A print-ready sheet opens in a new tab:

• Four cards per page, portrait, with dashed cutting guides.
• Each card shows the branded panel, the value, a scannable barcode plus the written code, the serial number, and the validity terms. Complimentary cards additionally show who they were issued to, the issue date, and the expiry.

Print dialog settings — the cause of almost every printing complaint:

• Pick the correct paper size (A4 or US Letter) in the console's toolbar.
• In the browser dialog, keep margins on default (or none) and scale at 100%.

Cards printing too small, or a blank page after each sheet, are scale-and-margin problems — fix them in the dialog, not the design.

The two printing rules.

• Sellable cards can be printed at any time. Printing them is how the counter is stocked — a printed, unsold sellable card carries no value until a sale binds payment to it, so printing ahead is safe and intended.
• Complimentary cards can be printed only after activation. This blocks two problems at once: an unauthorised batch cannot be printed at all, and the same card cannot be printed twice by mistake — two identical printed copies of one live card would be two claims on one balance.

Summary. Activate: open batch → select cards (partial is normal) → issued-to and reason (printed on the card) → Activate, which stamps the approver and sets the dates. Print: four per page with cut guides; paper size in the toolbar; margins default, scale 100%. Sellable prints anytime; complimentary only after activation.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The counter, the register, and the Overview
lessons.html:
Selling at the counter. Two situations, both from module 4's voucher sale, completed here with the console's view:

• A printed card. The cashier scans the barcode or types the code at payment. The sale marks the card Sold and starts its validity from that day. The customer can be emailed a copy automatically when the sale completes — and if the email never arrives, it can be re-sent from that sale's record.
• A blank card (no pre-printed code). The till assigns a fresh code at the moment of payment — common amounts offered, any amount typeable — and prints it on the spot. Cards created this way are grouped into the day's till batch, so at close they can be reconciled: cards issued at this till today against voucher payments taken today. That daily check is on module 8's routine.

Either way, the code, the value owed and the expiry are recorded identically — the console shows one consistent picture regardless of how the card was born.

Redemption. A presented card pays down the purchase and its balance falls: partly used → Partially redeemed; used up → Redeemed. The profile's partial-redemption and change-policy settings (module 2) govern the arithmetic; the offline policy (Online Only, or Guarded Offline within its caps) governs availability.

The register (Vouchers). Every card, across all batches and companies:

• Search by code, serial, or the issued-to name. Filter by company, type and state.
• The list shows each card's code, type, state, face value, remaining balance, batch and expiry.
• Open any card for its detail page: value, balance, key dates, issue details, and a history of every event that changed its balance — the card's own ledger.
• From the detail page: reprint that single card (an authorised action — module 4's rule that the slip is handled like cash applies), and cancel (void) for cards lost, damaged or issued in error. Remember Chapter 2: void is permanent, a void card can never be redeemed, and the cancellation stays on the record. Replace a wrongly voided card with a new one; do not argue with the void.

The Overview. The programme at a glance, for one company or all:

• Total cards and batches.
• Outstanding value — what is currently owed to cardholders (the live liability).
• Value redeemed, and total face value ever issued.
• A breakdown by state where each figure is a link — click through to the matching card list.

The same figures feed the finance reports: the outstanding-liability statement, activity over a date range, and the lapsed-value summary that Chapter 7 uses.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The accounting and the monthly check
lessons.html:
Four events cover everything a voucher does financially. Learn the four postings and the whole programme's accounting is understood.

Event 1 — a gift card is sold. The cash received is recorded, and the same amount is credited to the liability account — value owed to the cardholder. It is not revenue, and no sales tax is charged.

Event 2 — a card is redeemed against goods. The liability is reduced by the amount spent, and the sale — with its tax — is recognised on the goods the customer takes. Revenue and tax arrive when goods leave, not when the promise was bought.

Event 3 — a complimentary card is redeemed. No money ever came in for this card, so its cost is recognised as a promotional expense at the point of redemption, in the account named in Setup (or the liability account if none was named). The giveaway is costed when it is actually used.

Event 4 — a card expires with value left. The remaining value is no longer owed. A finance manager recognises it as breakage income, clearing the stale liability from the books.

Breakage is a deliberate decision. Three facts about event 4:

• Recognition is a decision the Accounts Manager makes — the system never books breakage on its own.
• The system never records the same lapsed value twice — the sweep can be run safely.
• Choose the timing as part of the period routine (for example, sweep expired value quarterly), not ad hoc.

Why manual: automatic breakage would create income on a schedule nobody reviews, and it would conflict with reality — businesses sometimes honour an expired card as goodwill. Keeping recognition as a dated, named decision keeps the income real and reviewable.

The monthly check. Once a month, compare two numbers:

1. The programme's outstanding value — from the Overview, or from Gift Voucher Analytics on the till side (which also shows active vouchers, sold and redeemed in the period, and the redemption rate).
2. The balance of the liability account in the books.

They should agree, or the difference should be explainable. While checking, read three more things: the redemption rate (cards coming back is the programme working), the liability trend (December's sales are January's obligations — plan for the redemption wave), and the expired-with-balance pipeline (value awaiting the next breakage decision).

Guarded Offline, revisited. If the profile chose Guarded Offline (module 2), the offline caps — largest single voucher, daily total per terminal — are the one place the register and reality can briefly disagree during an outage. The caps were set as an affordable exposure; the monthly check is where any such disagreement surfaces and is resolved.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The monitoring reads; worked example: Okelewo's December
lessons.html:
Vouchers are portable value, so the programme carries specific risks. Each has a built-in control and a simple check. Run the checks on the routine given; none takes more than minutes.

1. Unauthorised activation. Risk: a complimentary batch made live outside any planned campaign. Control: the activation gate — every activation carries its approver's name. Check (monthly): read the activation log against the campaign plan; every activated batch should match a known giveaway.

2. Duplicate issue. Risk: two tills issuing the same code, leaving two customers holding one balance. Control: Enforce Voucher Booking (module 2) reserves each code centrally before issue; the printing rule also prevents double-printing complimentary cards. Check: redemption failures — a cluster of already-redeemed errors is the signature of this problem.

3. Buy-back misuse. Risk: the buy-back switch (voucher redeemed for cash) used to pump stored value out of the drawer. Control: leave buy-back off (Okelewo: off permanently); where a business insists on it, require an override. Check (weekly, if enabled): buy-back count and value per till per cashier — the healthy figure is near zero, and any trend needs an explanation.

4. Void after redemption. Risk: value spent, then the card voided to muddy the record. Control: the void is permanent, named, and kept; the card's history shows every balance event in order. Check (monthly): voids by author and by prior state — a void on a partially redeemed card deserves a look.

5. Phantom blank-card sales. Risk: blank cards coded at a till without genuine payment. Control: till-issued cards group into the day's till batch. Check (daily, at close): the till batch against voucher payments taken — cards issued must match money received; any gap is investigated that evening.

6. Complimentary leakage. Risk: giveaway cards drifting to staff, friends and family. Control: issued-to and reason notes, printed on the card; partial activation limited to the campaign's count. Check (monthly): complimentary redemption patterns — repeated names, staff overlaps, one branch out of line.

7. Role overlap. Risk: one person able to create value, sell it, and account for it. Control: the role separation from Chapter 1. Check (at the periodic access review): who holds Voucher Manager, who holds Accounts Manager, and that counter staff hold neither.

Okelewo's December. The launch, in order: Setup first — the accountant wires both accounts, all four validations pass, and the MD's plan to count voucher sales as December revenue is corrected in one meeting with Chapter 3's rule (his conclusion: so it is a loan from customers who intend to spend it here. I can live with that loan). Design by the guided route. Generate: three sellable denominations matching the profile's quick buttons, plus 500 complimentary cards for the season's promotion. Import: leftover 2024 experiment cards brought in by serial range — printed numbers kept as codes, arriving inactive like everything else. Activation: 120 of the 500, issued-to and reason recorded, the approver stamp checked once as a drill. Printing: one sheet wasted learning the scale-at-100% rule, none after. The counter: both selling routes run all month, and the nightly till-batch check reconciles every day. January: the first monthly check matches the Overview's outstanding value to the liability account within rounding; the redemption rate is healthy; the breakage decision for the imported legacy cards is scheduled for their expiry quarter. The accountant's note: it is a small bank — cards out, value owed, books that agree. Which is what it always was; now the records exist.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & module rule 7
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

The programme (Chapter 1). A voucher is a promise of value — money owed until spent or expired. The console at /vouchers: Overview, Batches, Vouchers, Generate, Import, Design, Setup. Roles: Voucher Manager (runs the console), Administrator, Accounts Manager (accounts and breakage), counter staff (till only). Keep creating, handling and accounting separated.

Kinds, states, the gate (Chapter 2). Sellable: ready at creation, clock from sale. Complimentary: inactive at creation, activated by a manager, clock from activation — so a stolen or premature batch cannot be redeemed. Six states: Available, Sold, Partially redeemed, Redeemed, Expired, Void. Void is permanent and stays on record. Every card keeps a balance and a serial number for life.

Setup (Chapter 3). Liability account (every sale credits it — never revenue, never taxed at sale) and optional promotional expense account. Choose accounts (validated on company, kind, posting, active) or Create defaults for me (accounts, product, tax treatment, payment method in one step). Revenue and tax are recognised at redemption, on the goods. Booking voucher sales as revenue creates four errors at once. Setup before the first batch.

Design and creation (Chapter 4). Branded left half (guided or custom), standard right half. The preview uses the real print engine; no design falls back to a neutral panel. Generate: type, company, one value per batch, up to 10,000, validity at creation. Import: serials pasted or as ranges (0001-0500); printed numbers stay the redemption codes; imports arrive as inactive complimentary batches.

Activation and printing (Chapter 5). Open batch → select (partial is normal) → issued-to and reason (printed on the card) → Activate: approver recorded, dates set, cards move to Sold. Printing: four per page with cut guides; paper size in the toolbar; margins default, scale 100%. Sellable prints anytime (stocking); complimentary only after activation (no unauthorised print, no double print).

Counter and register (Chapter 6). Printed cards scan-to-sell with validity from that day and a re-sendable email copy. Blank cards get a fresh code at payment and join the day's till batch for the close reconciliation. The register finds any card by code, serial or name; the detail page shows the balance history, reprints (authorised), and the permanent void. The Overview's figures link through to card lists.

Accounting (Chapter 7). Four events: sale → liability, no tax; redemption → sale and tax on the goods; complimentary redemption → promotional expense; expiry → breakage income, recognised by a finance manager's deliberate decision — never automatic, never double-counted. Monthly: outstanding value against the liability account, plus the redemption rate, the liability trend, and the expired-value pipeline.

The checks (Chapter 8). Activation log vs campaign plan; already-redeemed clusters; buy-back near zero; voids by author and prior state; the nightly till-batch match; complimentary redemption patterns; the role census.

Module rule 7: a voucher is money the business owes, tracked from creation to expiry. Module 8 closes the track: offline, the queue, the daily checks and supervision.

honest_counter.title: POS 8 — Daily Verification & Offline Operations
honest_counter.desc: Daily verification and offline operation: offline's works/waits boundary, the indicators and the queue worked to zero, conflicts re-picked and failed sales never deleted into silence, the fast-checkout decision, End of Day Funds and the five-step daily routine, the nine supervisor watch-patterns with their checks, the routine calendar with the change procedures, the annual handover drill, and the owner's five-number page — closing the ZhiftPOS Professional track.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The daily verification routine
lessons.html:
Seven modules configured the counter; this module covers its ongoing verification. It covers offline operation, the sales queue, the daily and weekly checks, and what supervisors watch for. It is the track's second ten-chapter module, and its module rule: the counter is checked daily, by routine — not by suspicion.

The module's two halves.

• Chapters 2-5: the system's side. Offline mode and its limits, the status indicators and the queue, conflicts and failed sales, and the fast checkout setting. A counter whose queue and postings are not managed cannot be reconciled, however honest its people.
• Chapters 6-7: the people's side. The end-of-day money check, and the specific patterns supervisors look for. Perfect machinery that nobody reads proves nothing.

Then the structure that keeps both running: the routine calendar and the staff/terminal change procedures (Chapter 8), the handover test and the owner's summary page (Chapter 9), and the review (Chapter 10).

Why this module and module 2 are the two big ones. Module 2 wrote the counter's rules — every power a decided setting. This module proves the rules are working — every balance counted, every queue cleared, every check owned. Rules without checking drift; checking without rules is guesswork. The six modules in between are the daily trading those two hold up.

Three working principles for everything ahead.

1. Read the counter, don't guess at it. The indicators, the reports and the variance figures replace impressions. When something seems wrong, the first move is always a specific screen, named in this module.
2. Every check is a comparison. Expected against counted, register against books, issued against received. A check that compares nothing proves nothing.
3. Work every list to zero. The queue, the conflicts, the failed sales, the unexplained variances. A healthy counter is not one with no discrepancies — it is one where every discrepancy has an owner, an age, and an ending.

What this buys. Module 1 opened with Okelewo's MD managing three shops by suspicion. This module ends with the same MD reading five numbers a week. The distance between those two states is exactly the routines in the next nine chapters — none of which takes more than minutes a day. And the order matters: the system's side comes first because the people's side depends on it — a variance report built on an undrained queue accuses nobody accurately, and an End of Day figure that excludes yesterday's failed sales proves less than it appears to. Get the machinery clean, then read the people's numbers with confidence.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Offline: what works and what waits
lessons.html:
When the connection drops, the top bar shows Offline and selling continues from the local copy — scanning at full speed, sales queuing on the terminal, receipts printing with local references. The basic sale feels identical, which is why the boundary must be learned: the till will not remind you of it until you cross it.

What works offline.

• Cash sales, manually keyed card sales, and transfer sales — tenders that just record an amount.
• Holds and resumes.
• Label printing.
• Lookups against the cached catalogue and cached customers.
• Voucher activity, only where the profile chose Guarded Offline, and only within its caps.

What waits for the connection.

• Store credit — the balance lives on the server; offline it reads as nothing and cannot be spent.
• Loyalty redemption — same reason: the points balance is the server's.
• Vouchers under the default Online Only policy.
• Integrated card payments — the device needs a live call. Use cash, keyed card, or transfer instead.
• Credit and part-paid sales — offline, collect the full amount. A balance the till cannot check cannot be extended.
• Return & Exchange — the original invoice, loyalty ledger and balances are on the server.
• Reports — the figures are the server's.

The whole table compresses to one rule: anything that depends on a balance or record only the server can verify, waits. Every refusal in the list is that rule applied to one feature. The refusals are the design working — the till never guesses at money it cannot check.

Running the counter offline — four habits.

1. Tell the queue what still works. One sentence when the banner flips: cash, transfer and card by machine are fine; returns and account payments when the connection is back. Announced once, the boundary causes no confusion.
2. Trust the queue. Queued sales are safe, survive restarts, and post on their own when the line returns. Do not restart anything to help them.
3. Watch the duration. An hour offline is normal operation. Most of a day is a connectivity incident — tell whoever manages the network, at whatever threshold the branch sets.
4. Check the lists when the connection returns. As the queue drains, look at the Conflicts and Failed indicators (Chapter 4). The outage is not over until both are clear — a drained queue with an unread conflict list is a day that only looks finished.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The indicators and the queue
lessons.html:
Module 4 listed the top-bar indicators; this chapter is about reading them as a set, and managing the one number that matters most: the queue.

The healthy pattern. Glance at the top bar and a healthy till shows: Online, no Re-login marker, Queued at or near zero, no Conflicts, no Failed, stock and price copies fresh, and Duty Active with a shift open. Learn that pattern; anything different is one of the specific situations below.

• Offline — expected during an outage. If the network is fine and only this terminal is offline, suspect the terminal: its sync service may have stopped (the same cause behind a stale last-seen in module 3).
• Re-login required — a specific cashier's stored credentials were rejected. That cashier's queued sales cannot post until they sign in online. Deal with it the same day: find the person, have them sign in.
• Stock stale / Price stale — the local copies are ageing. Click to sync. If staleness keeps recurring on one terminal, check its sync service and its cache limit (module 3).
• Queued climbing — see below.
• Conflicts / Failed — Chapter 4's worked lists.

Reading the queue. The queue rises while offline (every completed sale joins it) and drains when online (the sync service posts in order). So judge it by direction and age, not size alone:

• Thirty queued during an outage — normal; the design working.
• Thirty queued an hour after the connection returned — a stall. Check, in order: the sync service running? a Re-login marker blocking someone's sales? a Conflict at the head of the queue?
• A queue that never quite reaches zero — a counter permanently behind its own books.

Why the queue is worked to zero. Queued sales are safe — but they are money the books have not seen yet. Until the queue is empty, the back office's figures for the day are incomplete, and every report and reconciliation built on them is provisional. The rule, applied at three points:

1. At shift close — glance at Queued before counting. A non-zero queue means the close's expected figures and the books will disagree until it drains; note it in the closing notes.
2. At end of day — the supervisor's daily check (Chapter 6) starts with the queue at zero on every terminal. The end-of-day report is only final when the day has fully arrived.
3. Weekly — the pattern of queue behaviour across days is a connectivity report. A branch whose queue spikes every evening at the same hour has a network pattern to fix, not a cashier problem.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Conflicts and failed sales
lessons.html:
Two lists sit between the queue and the books. The rule for both, from the manual: conflicts and failed sales are real money that has not reached the books — clear them before the shift closes.

Conflicts. A sale completed offline (or during the posting gap) may name a batch or serial that another till sold in the meantime. The back office will not deduct the same physical stock twice, so it holds the sale back, and it appears under the Conflicts indicator.

Resolving one:

1. Click the Conflicts indicator and open the held sale. The refused line is shown.
2. Re-pick the batch or serial from what is actually available. (The goods physically left with the customer; the record just needs to point at an equivalent unit that is genuinely in stock.)
3. Release the sale. It posts normally.

A conflict is not a fault. It is the honest outcome of two tills selling from one stock pool with a connection in between — the alternatives (blocking all offline selling, or silently double-deducting stock) would both be worse. The cost is a minute of re-picking, paid occasionally.

Failed sales. A queued sale the back office rejected outright — a record deleted on the server, a validation the terminal could not know about, a posting error. These appear under the Failed indicator, and they are a supervisor's list: the causes live in the back office, beyond a cashier's reach.

Handling them:

1. Read the failure message and identify the cause. Patterns matter more than single cases: three failures on one item point at that item's data; three on one terminal point at that terminal.
2. Fix the cause, then re-submit the sale — or, where re-submission is impossible, formally re-enter the sale with a note referencing the original.
3. Never delete a failed sale into silence. The customer's money is already in the drawer; the books must eventually record the sale that produced it.

Age both lists. A conflict from this morning is routine work. A conflict from last Tuesday means the routine is not being followed — and that is the finding. Both lists are cleared as part of the shift close (module 4's counted drawer plus cleared lists equals a genuinely finished shift), and the weekly review looks at the totals: conflicts trending up suggests stock contention or connectivity worth examining; failures trending up suggests a data problem worth finding.

Summary. Conflict = re-pick and release, minutes, cashier-level. Failed = diagnose, fix, re-submit, supervisor-level, never silently removed. Both lists at zero before the shift closes; both trends read weekly.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Fast checkout: deciding the setting
lessons.html:
Module 3 said to leave fast checkout off at commissioning and decide it here, with the queue's behaviour understood. This chapter is that decision.

What it does. With fast checkout on, completing a sale returns the till to the next customer immediately — the sale posts to the back office in the background instead of the cashier waiting for confirmation. Scope:

• Applies to card, cash and transfer sales — the tenders that record an amount.
• Loyalty redemption still posts live — a server-verified balance keeps its verification. The other server-side tenders keep their online rules too.

The gain is real at a busy counter: a few seconds per sale, multiplied by a queue.

What it costs. A background posting can fail after the customer has left. The sale lands on Chapter 4's Failed list with the money already in the drawer and nobody standing at the counter to fix it. Fast checkout does not create errors — it moves their discovery from the cashier's eyes at the moment of sale to the Failed indicator afterwards. In other words, it widens the money-in-transit window this module exists to manage.

Where it fits. Turn it on for counters that are high-volume and low-exception:

• Fast-moving goods, Standard mode, simple tenders.
• Batches auto-allocated; serials rare.
• A history of few conflicts and few failures.

At such counters the seconds add up to real throughput and the failure rate stays near zero.

Where it does not fit. Leave it off for counters that are exception-rich:

• Serial-numbered goods, credit customers, heavy voucher traffic.
• A history of conflicts or failures.

Deferred confirmation multiplies exactly the cases that need eyes at the moment of sale.

Two conditions wherever it is on.

1. The Failed list is checked every shift, without exception. A failure found the same shift is a quick re-submission or re-ring; found a week later it is an investigation with a customer attached.
2. The decision is recorded — which terminals run fast checkout and why, noted with the terminal settings (module 3's file). The estate's fast-checkout map should be known, not discovered.

Summary. Fast checkout trades certainty-at-the-moment for speed, safely — but only where exceptions are rare and the Failed list is genuinely read every shift. Decide it per counter, write the decision down, and revisit it if the counter's failure pattern changes.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — End of Day Funds and the daily check
lessons.html:
The counter's money is proven daily, using two report screens and a fifteen-minute routine.

The two report screens.

• Command Center — the glance. Today's headline figures (gross sales, average basket, transactions, returns, invoices paid) with trend arrows, recent activity, top sellers, and the news ticker. For the floor and the manager's quick pulse through the day.
• Revenue Intelligence — the analysis. Four working reports: End of Day Funds (below), Detailed Sales (line-level sales over a range — margin and product-mix questions), Cashier Sales History (per-person trading records — Chapter 7 uses it), and Gift Voucher Analytics (module 7's programme figures). Access rides the money-side permissions — in Pharmacy mode, the Checkout access box carries it.

Routing rule: a how-are-we-doing question goes to the Command Center; a what-exactly-happened question goes to Revenue Intelligence.

End of Day Funds. The daily money proof. For the chosen day (or range), it lays out expected against counted, per shift and per payment method — the system's arithmetic beside the counts cashiers entered at their closes — with the surviving variances totalled.

Reading it:

• A day where every method reconciles is filed. Green and boring is the goal.
• A day with a variance is broken down in two clicks: which shift, which method. If the variance was explained in the shift's closing notes (module 4), the answer is already there. If not, it is tonight's question to a named person about a specific drawer — small, fresh, and answerable.

The daily routine. Run at end of day, in order:

1. Queues at zero on every terminal, and the Conflicts and Failed lists clear (Chapters 3-4). The day must have fully arrived before it can be proven.
2. Every shift closed with counted figures. Orphaned sales repaired with the back-office tool and noted — the tool is a correction, and its use should be rare.
3. End of Day Funds read, variances resolved against the closing notes or assigned to a named follow-up.
4. The voucher till batch reconciled — cards issued at the till today against voucher payments taken (module 7's daily check).
5. Cash banked or safed against the counted total — the day's money leaving the counter matches the day's proven figure.

Fifteen minutes, five steps, one filed result. The figures this routine proves are the same ones the accountant reconciles the bank against and the owner reads in Chapter 9 — a counter that runs this daily makes every downstream check in the business cheaper.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — What supervisors watch for
lessons.html:
This chapter lists the known counter-fraud patterns, each with the ZhiftPOS control that obstructs it and the specific check that catches what slips through. Supervisors should know all of them plainly. Two things to hold while reading: the checks exist to catch the rare bad case — and, just as much, to clear the honest majority with evidence. A counter that is checked weekly is a counter where good staff are never under vague suspicion.

1. Under-ringing. Goods leave for less than their price: an item not scanned for a friend, a cheaper item scanned in place of a dearer one, a quantity short-rung. Controls: serial and batch prompts resist substitution; every sale is line-recorded. Check: margin by cashier in Detailed Sales — a person whose baskets consistently earn less than the floor's mix suggests warrants a closer look, alongside their void pattern (point 4).

2. Drawer skimming. Cash taken from the drawer, hidden in the day's activity. Controls: the counted float and counted close — a skim must now survive two counts; per-method closing. Check: the variance trend per cashier. Everyone has an odd red day; the signal is drift — shortages that cluster on one person, or a cashier whose variances are suspiciously round or only ever negative.

3. Phantom returns. A refund processed with no customer and no goods — cash out against a fictional return. Controls: returns must start from a found invoice; a reason is required; an override can be required; cash refunds can be disabled entirely. Checks: returns per cashier (rate, and timing — returns clustering at shift end, or on the same day as the original sale), returns per customer (the Customer Desk's return-rate figure), and the cash-refund share where cash refunds are enabled.

4. Voids and cleared carts after payment. A customer pays; the sale is then voided or the cart cleared, and the cash is pocketed. Controls: cart clearing can require approval; voids and cleared carts are recorded. Check: voids and cleared carts per cashier per shift, especially adjacent to cash sales. This is the pattern shared logins used to make invisible; with individual accounts it is a report.

5. Discount misuse — and the rubber-stamp approver. Concessions granted to friends, or reasons gamed; and its quieter partner, the approver who approves everything asked. Controls: the discount modes, required reasons and explanations, budget percentages, the all-approvers code email. Checks: markdowns per cashier against budget (module 5's report), and approvals per approver — an approver clearing forty discounts a week is either the floor's only available approver (a staffing problem) or not reading what they sign (a supervision problem); the count says which question to ask.

6. Rate-edit habits. Prices rewritten line by line from memory as favours. Controls: the Rate override marker; the override requirement. Check: Rate override markers per cashier per week — Okelewo's Friday pattern in module 5 is the worked example.

7. Self-dealing on the arrangements. Store credit or refunds routed to accounts the cashier controls; staff-purchase or lay-by machinery bent toward friends; voucher self-issue. Controls: named-customer requirements, manager gates, the voucher role separation. Checks: refunds and credits by recipient, cross-read against the staff list; the lay-by and staff-purchase panels read for the same few names recurring.

8. Tender misrecording. Tenders recorded on the wrong method — carelessly (module 4's transfers-as-cash) or deliberately, to blur the per-method counts a skim would otherwise disturb. Controls: split payment records each portion on its method. Check: the method mix per cashier against the branch's normal pattern.

9. Working under another name. The shared-login habit returning, or manager-override sessions running long. Controls: individual accounts, the lock habit, tagged override sessions. Check: override sessions counted monthly — near zero, each with a known story — and sign-in patterns against the roster.

The weekly half-hour. Run the checks as a fixed circuit once a week: variance trends, returns and voids by cashier, markdowns against budget, approvals by approver, rate-edit markers, override sessions, and a glance at the arrangement panels. Log the result even when it is clean — a record of regular checking is itself a deterrent, and it is also the evidence that clears people. Most weeks the log says nothing found, and that sentence is worth having.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The routine calendar and the change procedures
lessons.html:
Every check in this track happens on a schedule someone owns. This chapter collects them into one calendar — the counter's standing routine — and adds the two change procedures and the update rule.

Each shift (the cashier).

• Count the float at open; declare anything unusual in the opening note.
• Glance at Queued, Conflicts and Failed before closing.
• Count the drawer at close; overwrite the pre-filled figures; explain variances in the notes.
• Handle voucher and airtime slips by their rules; lock the till at every step away.

Daily (the supervisor). The Chapter 6 routine: queues and lists at zero, shifts closed and counted, End of Day Funds read and resolved, the voucher till batch reconciled, cash banked against the count.

Weekly (the supervisor / branch).

• The Chapter 7 check circuit, logged.
• The Open Lay-Bys panel — overdue instalments followed up.
• The Open Staff Purchases panel — balances glanced.
• Every cashier signed in online on each terminal they use (the seven-day cache rule).
• Queue behaviour across the week read for connectivity patterns.

Monthly (the administrator / finance).

• The customer duplicate scan and merge (module 6).
• The voucher programme's outstanding value against the liability account (module 7), plus the redemption rate and the expired-value pipeline.
• The device list's last-seen review and the licence allowance check (module 3).
• Override sessions counted, each with its story.
• The voucher activation log against the campaign plan.

On staff change (same day). The three-record procedure from module 3 — profile rows removed, cached entries forgotten on every terminal they used (listed from the device register), the back-office account disabled — plus: remove them from the Power Approver table and from category-lead assignments if they held either.

On terminal change. Revoke the old device with who-and-why (the licence slot frees); commission the replacement by module 3's standard procedure; update the terminal file.

Updates. Install updates on the estate's decided posture (module 3), with two rules: never update a terminal with sales still in its queue — let the queue drain first — and stage updates across the estate rather than everywhere at once, noting the version. An update mid-queue is the one easily avoided way to turn Chapter 4's lists into a bad evening.

Write names on the calendar. Every line above has an owner: the cashier's lines by role, the daily and weekly lines usually the Sales Manager, the monthly lines split between the administrator and finance. A calendar with names survives holidays, resignations and busy seasons; a calendar in one person's head does not — which is exactly Chapter 9's test.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — The handover test and the owner's page; worked example: Okelewo
lessons.html:
The handover test. Ask this of any branch: if the best supervisor left this Friday, what would Monday look like? A counter run on this track's pattern passes, because nothing lives only in someone's head:

• The profiles are recorded decisions with noted reasons (module 2), not one person's memory of an afternoon of settings.
• The terminal estate is a register plus a file per terminal (module 3), not the-machines-someone-set-up.
• The routines are a calendar with names (Chapter 8), not habits that leave with their owner.
• The checks have a fixed circuit and a log with history (Chapters 6-7).
• A successor's first week is spent reading, not interviewing survivors.

Test it honestly once a year: a designated deputy runs the full weekly and monthly routine from the documentation alone, and every gap they hit is logged and fixed. The drill costs a morning. Discovering the gaps during a real departure costs a quarter.

The owner's page. Five numbers, readable in four minutes a week (or one a day), each backed by a screen the owner can open and a person whose name is on the line:

1. Yesterday's End of Day variance total, per branch — zero or explained is the only healthy state.
2. Queues, conflicts and failed sales right now — all zero? (The money-in-transit line.)
3. Overrides, voids and cleared carts this week, per branch — a trend line, not an incident report.
4. Voucher value outstanding and the month's redemption rate — the programme's health.
5. Margin per branch against last month — Detailed Sales' one-line answer on whether the discount controls are holding.

Okelewo at the end of the track. The opening problems, closed one by one: the exercise books are retired (two are framed on the flagship's back-office wall); the shared login is eleven individual accounts, a lock habit, and a monthly override count that reads near zero with stories; the memory prices are a governed price list, three discount modes matched to three floors, and a markdown report that names causes; the unreconciled drawers are counted floats, counted closes, and an End of Day report whose green days are filed unread because there is nothing in them; the unattributable returns pattern that started the whole project is now impossible to repeat — returns need an invoice, a reason and an approver, and the weekly circuit reads them by person. The MD's question from module 1 — what did any counter do on Tuesday? — now has an answer at every level: per branch, per terminal, per shift, per cashier, per method, per line, variances explained by name. The final meeting is short: the owner's page taught in twenty minutes, the calendar's names confirmed, the first handover drill scheduled. The MD's closing note: nine years of managing by suspicion, replaced by four minutes of reading. I just have to keep reading.

The certification. With this module, the ZhiftPOS Professional track is complete: eight modules, from the system's parts to the daily proof — the counter's rules in one hand, its checks in the other.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Review & module rule 8
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the final quiz of the track.

Offline (Chapter 2). Selling continues from the local copy; sales queue safely. Works: cash, keyed card, transfer, holds, labels, cached lookups, Guarded Offline vouchers within caps. Waits: store credit, loyalty redemption, Online Only vouchers, integrated card, credit and part-paid sales (collect the full amount), Return & Exchange, reports. One rule covers it all: whatever depends on a balance only the server can verify, waits. Four habits: announce what works, trust the queue, watch the duration, check the lists when the connection returns.

The indicators and the queue (Chapter 3). The healthy pattern: Online, no Re-login, Queued near zero, no Conflicts or Failed, copies fresh, Duty Active. Re-login blocks that cashier's queued sales — same-day fix. Judge the queue by direction and age: thirty during an outage is normal; thirty an hour after it is a stall (sync service, Re-login, or a conflict at the head). The queue is worked to zero: at shift close, at end of day, and read weekly for connectivity patterns.

Conflicts and failed sales (Chapter 4). A conflict = another till took the batch/serial: open, re-pick, release — minutes. A failed sale = the back office rejected it: a supervisor diagnoses, fixes, re-submits — never deleted into silence, because the money is already in the drawer. Both lists cleared before the shift closes; both trends read weekly; patterns (one item, one terminal) matter more than single cases.

Fast checkout (Chapter 5). Instant completion, background posting; card, cash and transfer only; loyalty still posts live. Cost: a failure can surface after the customer leaves. Fits high-volume, low-exception counters; does not fit serial-heavy, credit-heavy or conflict-prone ones. Two conditions where on: the Failed list read every shift, and the decision recorded per terminal.

The daily check (Chapter 6). Command Center = the glance; Revenue Intelligence = the analysis (End of Day Funds, Detailed Sales, Cashier Sales History, Gift Voucher Analytics). End of Day Funds: expected against counted, per shift and method. The five-step evening routine: queues and lists at zero, shifts closed, End of Day read and resolved, the voucher till batch reconciled, cash banked against the count.

The watch list (Chapter 7). Nine patterns — under-ringing, skimming, phantom returns, voids/cleared carts, discount misuse and the rubber-stamp approver, rate-edit habits, self-dealing, tender misrecording, working under another name — each with its control and its named check. The weekly half-hour circuit, logged even when clean; the checks clear the honest as much as they catch the rare bad case.

The calendar (Chapter 8). Per shift, daily, weekly, monthly; staff change (three records plus approver and lead tables, same day); terminal change (revoke, commission, file); updates never mid-queue, staged across the estate. Names on every line.

The finish (Chapter 9). The annual handover drill from documentation alone; the owner's five-number page; Okelewo's opening problems each closed by a specific routine.

Module rule 8: the counter is checked daily, by routine — not by suspicion. The track's eight module rules together: the counter runs on a profile, not memory; every power is a decided setting with an owner; a terminal is commissioned once and managed for life; the shift is a sealed routine; every discount and return carries a reason and an approver; every extended counter is a financial arrangement; a voucher is money owed, tracked from creation to expiry; and the counter is checked daily. That is the ZhiftPOS Professional certification.
